has this past year filled so well. He served as Inspecto r of District No. 625

session in 1970. His outstand ing leadersh ip qualities were further recognized when he was elected Junior Grand Warden in October of 1977. from
which station he progresse d through the Grand Lodge elective offices. culminating in his election as Grand Master in October of 1980.
Our Grand Master was born in Okmulge e. Okla homa May 29. 1925. His

their two daughter s, Debra and Linda and son Stephen . Doug and Maxine
have lived there in the same house since 1952. Currently our Grand Master
is manager and Chief Engineer of Gammalo y. Ltd .. a subsidiar y of the
Cree Oil Compan y in the city of Long Beach.
Typically. H. Douglas Lemons found time to serve his adopted city well
as Presiden t of th e C hamber of Commer ce while in the Grand Lodge line.
. Concerni ng Freemaso nry. he has always heen a firm advocate of changmg or removing laws and/or policies which have been found to he outdated
and counter-p roductive . always seeking new inspiratio nal methods and
program to strengthe n th e fraternal fiber of our C raft and to promote the
bonds of hrotherly love and affect ion among our members.
Illustrativ e of this dedicatio n. o ur Grand Master was the chief architect
and designer of th e popular "Layman 's Night Program ". designed to educate non-Mas ons to Freemaso nry's aims. purposes and goals. During this

A highlight of H . Douglas Lemons' year as Grand Master came when
he led a contingent of California Masons to Israel and Greece on the "first
Grand Masters Pilgrimage." There our Brethren visited the site of King
Solomon's Temple and other important Masonic locations in the Holy Land.
The bonds of fraternal love and respect between our Grand Lodge and
that of Israel were gre.atly strengthened by the personal friendships developed between our representatives and those of the Holy Land.
A firm believer and active supporter of the Masonic Youth Orders. our
Grand Master, during the past year alone, made more than forty personal
visitations to Bethels, Chapters and Assemblies, carrying along in his enthusiasm as many as 125 Brothers to signify our support of youth activities.
He was , incidentally, awarded the "Cross of Color" by the Rainbow Girls
at their Grand Assembly in Fresno. He was previously awarded the DeMolay
Legion of Honor in 1974.
Our Brother was raised a Master Mason. May 27. 1958 in Bixby Knolls
Neptune Lodge No. 699, Long Beach . and was honored by being elected
to serve his Lodge as Master in 1966. He joined the Scottish Rite in Long
Beach in 1967 and was honored by that body in 1975 with the 33rd degree,
Honorary Inspector General. Other Masonic affiliations include the Long
Beach York Rite Bodies, Al Malaikah Shrine Temple, El Bekal Shrine
Temple, Signal Hill High Twelve Club. Oranco Chapter of the Grotto. Red
Cross of C.onstantine, and honorary membership in all three Masonic Youth
Orders. During his year as Grand Master. Doug " rounded out" his memberships by joining the Order of the Eastern Star and the Royal Order of
the Amaranth.
One of his proudest accomplishmen ts this year was his instrumentality
in forming and instituting three new California Masonic Lodges: Alta California Research Lodge U.D. , Orange County Daylight Lodge U.D .. and
Square and Compass Lodge U.D.
H . Douglas Lemons' superlative devotion of mind. spirit and body to
the development and strengthening of unity and cooperation between all
Masonic bodies; his zeal and energetic pursuit of programs to educate and
inform Masons and non-Masons as to what Masonry stands for. what it is
and is not; his tireless and unselfish efforts to give always the best that is
in him for the benefit of the craft-all these set a goal for other Masons to
measure up to, to emulate , support. and in the future. by building on a
foundation so securely laid out. surpass. That is . surely. our Grand Master's fondest hope, and perhaps his greatest gift of all to the Craft he loves.
as well as to each of us who serve the cause of Freemasonry. country, and
God .
Thank you, Most Worshipful.

MEMORIAL SERVICE
DEVOTIONAL AND NECROW GY

What I have just read was the result of King Solomon's prayer request
as he entered the solemn responsibilities of his kingship. All through his
magnificent reign Solomon was a man of prayer. When I pondered .. the
.implications of this prayer experience of this man and his special significance to Masonry, I felt divinely impelled to focus on the subject of prayer
for this Annual Communication. In my thinking, prayer is one of the most
important things we do as Masons. Why do I say that? Let me recall to
your minds these words intoned by the Master at the opening and beginning of every Masonic function:
"In accordance with the teachings of our Institution, it is our duty before
entering upon any great or important undertaking, to invoke the aid
and blessing of God. We shall, therefore, reverently unite with our chaplain in an address to the Throne of Grace."
The words are familiar to all of us, are they not? Now, then, is this
important thing we do merely an observance of a ritual, a perfunctory act
we perform on command? It could readily be, unless we understand the
meaning and purpose of our prayers. I want us to reflect for a few moments
on meaning and purpose.
_
First of all, I believe we need to explore what prayer really is; it will
carry no significance with it if we do not understand. In simple yet profound words a great hymn describes it thus:

Invocation

As brother Masons from near and far we have gathered, Great Architect
and Supreme Ruler of the Universe, to conduct the affairs of the 132nd
Communication of the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the
State of California and Hawaii. We now open our hearts and minds to Thy
Holy Presence and Divine Guidance. Sustain us throughout the deliberations of this season. May what is said and done here receive your sanction
and blessing.
In gratitude we lift our hearts to Thee, Author of Light and Life, for
the privilege of being part of the family of Masons which today has opportunity, by virtue of its cardinal principles and precepts, to bring light
in the midst of darkness, b1rotherly love into the scenes of hatred and
violence, and hope wherever there is despair.
"Grant us Thy peace throughout our
earthly life,
Our balm in sorrow and our stay in
strife;
Then when Thy voice shall bid our
conflict cease,
Call us, 0 Lord, to thine eternal peace." Amen.
Devotional
Most Worshipful Grand Master and Members of the Grand Lodge:
Scripture Reading from the Third Chapter of the First Book of Kings,
verses four through sixteen.
"The Lord was pleased that Solomon had asked for this, and so he said
to him, 'Because you have asked for the wisdom to rule justly, instead
of long life for yourself or riches or the death of your enemies, I will do
what you asked. I will give you more wisdom and understanding than
anyone has ever had or will have again .. .' "

"Prayer is the soul's sincere desire,
Unuttered or expressed,
The motion of a hidden fire
That trembles in the breast.
Prayer is the burden of a sigh,
The falling of a tear,
The upward glancing of an eye,
When none but God is near.
Prayer is the simplest form of speech
That infant lips can try;
Prayer the sublimest strains that
Reach the Majesty on high."
From these poetic strains I deduce that prayer is a dialogue; a coming
together (Communion); a sharing of our thoughts and feelings with the
One in whom we live and move and have our being, the One we believe
and trust. A quick review of biblical history reinforces this definition. We
find that the ancient Hebrew patriarchs, prophets and sages continually
pour out their hearts and minds to the God of their faith. This God of
theirs was no figment of their imagination. To them He was a living reality.
John Shelby Spong in his book, "Honest Pray.er" spells this reality out for
us:
"God, to the biblical mind was a Force with which to reckon, a Power
to be engaged, a Reality to be experienced. To have faith, for the He-

7

8

9

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

brew, was not to do some mental activity like believing, it was rather,
to possess the ability to enter life expectantly, confident that God was
to be found there."

A final wo~d I "'.ant to share with you is a personal component that
should b~ resident in. o.ur prayers. By this I mean that in prayer there is
the meeting of the divine and the human, the divine responding to the
pers~mal needs and co~cerns of the human. The prayer dialogue will have
special perso.nal meaning when we understand that. Let me say that God
does something for us ~nd to us w~en we engage Him seriously and reveren~ly.. We catch .a ghmpse of this personal dimension in the Evening
Meditation of David, the Poet Laureate of Israel in Psalm 8:

For a sense of this reality, we have prime evidence of it in the Book of
the Psalms that are replete with prayers spoken out of human desperation,
and contain for us excellent models when we are stuck for the proper
expressions in our prayer life. What this teaches us is that all our prayers
must have in them the component of sensing the God to whom we direct
our prayers as a present Reality. It must be so, otherwise we are in the
overt act of talking to ourselves! Thus in the light of biblical background,
this is what it means to engage ourselves in the act of prayer.
A second thing of import I want to say relative to prayer, is that we
need to understand Who it is we direct our prayers to. Our prayers will
have absolutely no meaning unless they are rooted in the theological assumption that there is One who listens to us. A cardinal principle in the
Masonic belief system is the belief in a Supreme Being. What we say, think
and feel, we believe is committed to a Personal Being who cares and
responds to our personal needs and requests.
The magnificent and inspiring language of Masonry describes this One
toward whom we direct our prayers. Let me recall for a moment our modes
of address:
"Great Architect of the Universe!"
"Supreme Ruler of the Universe!"
"Maker and Ruler of all Worlds!"
"Author of Light and Life!"
"Great Source of Love and Happiness!"
"Supreme Grand Master!"
These are the exclamations of awe and respect of every Mason who
holds firmly to the belief in the God of his faith. These are affirmations
we exclaim with every fiber of our heart and mind.
From time to time, I have experienced twinges of disrespect when a
brother Mason facetiously refers to the God of his faith as, "The Man
Upstairs," or "The Big Boss in the Sky." I do not think that becoming the
language and character of Masonry. Brethren, before such demeaning utterances, let us remember who we are really addressing!
This God with whom we dialogue in our prayers is the One, who out of
the void and chaos of the Universe, brought a world of order and design,
the one in whom we live, move, and have our being. Reflect for a moment
with me upon the awe-inspiring beginning of things as recorded in the
Book of Genesis (1:1-5):
"In the beginning when God created the universe, the earth was formless
and desolate. The raging ocean that covered everything was engulfed in
total darkness and the power of God was moving over the water. Then
God commanded, 'Let there be light' and the light appeared. God was
pleased with what he saw..."

"Wh~n I consid~r the heavens, the moon and the stars which Thou hast
ordaine~; wh.at 1s man that Thou doest care for him ... For Thou has
mad~ ~1m a httle less than Thyself for Thou hast given Him power and

dom1mon over the land, the sea and the sky and all things that pass
through them. 0 Lord God, how excellent is Thy Name in all the earth."
In closing this meditation, I believe it would be fitting to close with the
prayer from the Man of Galilee in word and song to commemorate the
Grand Master's Pilgrimage to the Holy Land last Spring, the place where
this hallowed Galilean taught his disciples and followers the art of prayer.

EULOGY
PAUL A. PFLUEGER

By Robert T. Gilmore, Jr.
Paul, a native of San Francisco, began his banking life at the age of 14
with the Old Humboldt Bank. He advanced in position to Senior VicePresident of the Bank when it consolidated with the United Security Bank
and Trust Company. He later negotiated the merger of that firm with the
Bank of America. In 1928 he started a new career with an investment firm
which later bore his name. He retired from an active business life in 1973.
Brother Pflueger also served for many years as Governor of the Pacific
Coast Stock Exchange, President of the San Francisco Shopping News and
was Western National Vice-President of the National Association of Credit
Management. He was a Past President of Lake Merced Golf and Country
Club and a member of the Bohemian Club. Brother Pflueger was a Past
Master of Amity Lodge, served as the first Assistant Grand Treasurer from
1949 until 1964. In May 1964 he was appointed Grand Treasurer and served
with distinction until October, 1971. Brother Pflueger also served Grand
Lodge as Treasurer of the Masonic Homes and as a member of the Board
of Trustees of the California Masonic Memorial Temple. Paul A. Pflueger,
a prominent San Francisco banker and investment counselor for nearly 70
years and a distinguished Mason was called from "labor" on April 9, 1981
at the age of 90. A Memorial Service was held in the Grand Lodge Auditorium.
We will now have the special eulogy for Past Grand Master John F.
Roberts, Jr.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

11

EULOGY
JOHN F. ROBERTS, JR.

By Rev. Haven Martin

JOHN FERGUSON ROBERTS, JR.
Grand Master
October 16, 1975-0ctober 14, 1976
BORN
February 22, 1910
Cheyenne, Wyoming

DIED
February 1, 1981
Palo Alto, California

It is my high honor and privilege to share with you my thoughts concerning the life and service of the Most Worshipful John Ferguson Roberts,
Jr., and may I begin by quoting from the 1976 Proceedings of this Grand
Lodge: "The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons
of the State of California was indeed fortunate to have as its l lOth Grand
Master, during our Nation's Bicentennial Year, a man who has proven to
be of the same quality as some of the great founders of our nation. His
wisdom, courage and understanding have been a trademark that will long
remain after his service is completed." This trademark still remains after
his service on this earth has ended. I commend for your reading the item
on John Roberts at the beginning of the 1976 Proceedings, and will not try
to repeat the information contained in it, but rather just comment on it.
Although physically, John was not a tall man and was often told in good
humor to stand up while speaking, he stood very tall in every area of
service in which he engaged.
His engineering career, following his graduation from Stanford University in 1932, was one of rapid advancement and recognition of his knowledge and dedicatjon to the profession for which he had been trained. After
his retirement in 1975 John continued to serve as a consultant, sharing his
experience with those who had need of his special skills.
His career as a Mason also shows his dedication and commitment to the
principles of Freemasonry, and it was his great desire to share with others
that which he had learned. This was his motivation to serve as Master of
his Lodge, Inspector of his District, in Grand Lodge through the Elected
Line and as Grand Master, and his continuing service as Past Grand Master. He upheld the highest ideals of Freemasonry, not only in his adherence
to its principal tenets and its cardinal virtues, but also in representing that
spirit of brotherhood which arises from the recognition that the whole human species is one family for we are all the children of one Almighty
Parent. Whether we thought of John as the Most Worshipful, or thought
of him as a friend, we knew we were a part of the same brotherhood as
John F. Roberts, Jr.
The Grand Chapter of California, Order of the Eastern Star, also recognized his spirit of brotherhood and love of fraternity. In 1978 he served
the Grand Chapter as Grand Chaplain, and for the year 1981 he was elected
Associate Grand Patron and in just about ten days from today would have ·
been elected and installed Worthy Grand Patron.

12

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Among his many great services as a Master Mason is the service he gave
to the Masonic Youth Groups. He started his career as a member of the
Masonic family in DeMolay, and served as Master Councilor of Salinas
Chapter in 1928. He was awarded the Active DeMolay Legion of Honor
in 1973, and at the time of his death was serving as Assistant Executive
Officer for the Northern California Division of DeMolay. He also served
many times on the Rainbow Advisory Board and the Job's Daughters
Guardian Council in Palo Alto, and had been honored with the Rainbow
Grand Cross of Colors.
John had a faith in God, as required of all Masons, but he demonstrated
and practiced that faith through very active service to his church, The First
United Methodist Church of Palo Alto, where he served as Sunday School
Superintendent, on the Educational Committee, Finance Committee and
Board of Trustees, and was a leader among the members of these committees and boards. He recognized that his participation in the church was the
source of strength and understanding for the many other activities in which
.
he engaged, and the services which he rendered.
John stood tall as a family man, and John and Alice made a team from
their marriage in 1936 to the last moment of his life among us. A very close
and loving family included three daughters, one son, and fourteen grandchildren.
The Most Worshipful John F. Roberts, Jr., entered the life immortal on
February 1, 1981, and a Memorial Service, including the Masonic Funeral
Service conducted by Past Grand Master Vernon L. Gordon, was held on
February 5, 1981, at the Stanford University Chapel. Brothers, sisters and
friends from all over this Grand Jurisdiction filled the Chapel to overflowing.
In closing, may I quote and paraphrase a bit the closing words of the
article on John Roberts in the 1976 Proceedings:
"Past Grand Master John F. Roberts, Jr., the friendship so freely given by
you and Alice through the years has created a new dimension of happiness
in our Fraternity, and your continuing spiritual presence among us will
bring many of us a little closer to our God. We commend you, Johnny, for
a life well lived and a job well done."
Now that we are about to draw closed the sable curtains of this Memorial, let us rise, clasp the hands with the Brothers on each side, ever remembering that we are bound together by an indissoluble chain of sincere
affection. In memory of our departed Brethren, may this bond tightly embrace the entire globe, our beloved Fraternity as it does in our Masonic
Memorial Temple.

GENE AUTRYo
Brother Gene Autry, star of many Western movies was escorted into

CASS HARE
STATE DEPUTY, KNIGHTS OF COLUMBUS•
At the invitation previously extended by the Grand Master, Mr. Cass
Hare, State Deputy of the Knights of Columbus, was escorted into Grand
Lodge and addressed those in attendance. The theme ~f his message was
that the basic precepts of his organization and the Masonic Fraternity are
very similar. Both strive to drive out evil from our country and fill it with
good. The Knights of Columbus and the Masons share a common cause
-unity without uniformity and that this unity must remain steadfast now
and forever. A standing ovation was accorded his inspirational message.
TRIBUTE TO THE AMERICAN FLAG
BY-JUNIOR GRAND DEACON, ROYAL DANO•
A nation conceived in liberty, born out of faith in God, and dedicated
to the proposition that all men are created equal and thus entitled to
freedom .
It is with this freedom in mind that we pause at the very beginning of
this Grand Communication to pay tribute to this flag which represents
every freedom of this country.
Freedom that has brought to its people a degree of prosperity and happiness never even approached under any other banner.
A country which derives its just powers from the consent of the governed.
A country with a constitution that is the greatest single document in the
entire struggle of mankind for orderly self-government.
These blessings come not without cost. Throughout our brief history as
a nation, when danger has threatened, millions of Americans have left
their homes and families to defend this flag and the nation for which it
stands. Some never to return. Yet they are here embraced forever within
her folds . For their purity is remembered in her stripes of white.
Their blood has given her stripes of red.
Their souls are cradled in her stars.
And their courage embedded in her blue.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

At this moment, while our flag flies at peace in turbulent times, men
and women from nations around the world risk their lives; trudging
through arid deserts parched with thirst, crossing shark infested waters in
leaky hulks, crawling through minefields, barbed wire, past gun emplacements over seemingly unsurmountable walls, to reach these shores, to
touch and stand beside -This Symbol of Liberty.
This Rallying Point of Man's Dreams!
This Standard of Justice!
This Banner of the Rights of Man!
This emblem of man's faith!
This Light of Humanity!
This Beacon shining into the darkness!
This Flag of the United States of America!!
October 12, 1981 this Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California and our Brothers of Hawaii do
now dedicate themselves to the same love of country, devotion to freedom
and unfaltering ideals of those founding fathers that have made this country the Hope of Mankind.

GRAND MASTER'S MESSAGE

(•Note: Recorded here for convenience)

23

My Brethren:
I approach this moment, the end of a most enjoyable, challe~ging, a~d
rewarding year, with mixed feelings of satisfaction and frustration-satisfaction with the tremendous cooperation and help given me, incalculable
assistance which has made it possible to accomplish the achievements of
this wonderful, never-to-be-forgotten year-and frustration in leaving undone so many things to be done.
I would be sadly remiss if I did not specifically express my deepest, most
heartfelt gratitude to all the hundreds and thousands of people-good,
faithful, devoted, and dedicated members of our great Masonic familyall of whom have been so helpful; so constant and cordial in their friendship; so constructive in their suggestions, counsel, and guidance during my
years in the elective Grand Lodge Stations. To name them ~ndividually
would require an inordinate amount of time, for they are legion. Therefore, to all of you-and to those who are not present-I ask you, most
humbly and sincerely, to accept these meager words as a token of my
monumental appreciation and boundless gratitude for all that you have
done for me, personally, and for Freemasonry as well.
I understand that my feelings of satisfaction and frustration are common
to all individuals who assume great responsibilities.
Each Grand Master brings to the Station, the ideas he has formulated
in the past, in the hope that they may resolve all problems, situations, and
difficulties. During the preparatory years, he studies his predecessors, analyzes the problems, and devises plans for his administrative year. Unlike
the harried family breadwinner who always discovers there is too much
month for his income, the new administrator finds there is not enough year
to accomplish all his hopes and plans.
And so it is with me today. While I have some satisfaction with what
has been done, I also feel some frustration that the year has passed so
quickly-it has just been too short! There are so many things that need to
be done, that I wish I could have done, and that, now, I must leave to my
successors. This is life-unavoidable, consistent, and an ever present element of life. I recognize that I must now pass on the mantle of office, not
merely to one successor, but to a long line of successors. With it, I transfer
also my most fervent hope and prayer that Freemasonry will continue to
flourish in California, and that it will survive worldwide as "AN INSTRUMENT OF UNITY," bringing to all mankind the "PEACE AND HARMONY" that prevail within our Lodges.
As most of you know, the Grand Lodge theme for this year has been,
"FREEMASONRY, AN INSTRUMENT OF UNITY." Throughout this
year, it has been the constant guiding light of this administration. At every
turn, on each occasion, and at every opportunity, UNITY has been the
dominant thought.
This aim of Unity has been applied not only to our Constituent Lodge~,
but also to ALL of the organizations which make up our great Masonic

24

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

family. It has extended into all the communities which we have been privileged to visit, and has been applied to ALL the situations which we have
encountered.
One of the most thrilling and heartwarming demonstrations of "FREEMASONRY, AN INSTRUMENT OF UNITY," occurred on May 1st and
2nd of this year at the Conference of the Three Californias-our Grand
Lodge and the Grand Lodges of Baja California Del Norte and Baja
California Sur. At that meeting in Long Beach, the Fraternal bonds transcended the language barrier as the spontaneous friendliness and courtesy
melded the three groups into one large and happy family. Unity was not
merely exemplified-it was personified! Sincere cordiality was everywhere!
It was an indescribably glorious feeling, no, Reality-that permeated that
group.
Another event which occurred in June of this year very clearly demonstrates that borders and jurisdictions do not even exist when the spirit
of Unity prevails. I refer to the Oklahoma Indian Outdoor degree held in
Brea, California, June 6th, sponsored by Camellia Lodge No. 805 of Temple City. I have never seen the tenets of Masonry more proudly displayed!
There on a dusty baseball diamond, in the blazing afternoon sun, 2,500
Masons joined their hearts and their minds in a day of true Masonic fellowship. Two completely different Jurisdictions became as one under the
influence of Brotherly Love and understanding. We were indeed united!
And again, on June 28th, the spirit of Unity was magnificently displayed
when the Presiding Officers of all twenty-one of the Masonically affiliated
bodies came together as one in an All Masonic Family reception in Los
Angeles. Utilizing the wonderful facilities of the Al Malaikah Shrine Temple, the Heads of all these Masonically oriented bodies paid tribute to
Constituent Lodge Masonry, and told an audience of nearly 6,000 a little
about their individual organizations, their goals, aims, and purposes. The
feeling of all who were present that day was much like having attended a
family reunion-The Family of Masonry.
It would be totally impossible for me to express the full extent of my
feelings of admiration and respect for the leaders and members of all our
concordant Masonic bodies for the total support and cooperation which
they have given me and the Grand Lodge this year. Because of their
efforts, true progress is being made in many areas.
For the Grand Lodge Officers, the year 1980--81 has been a year of
travel. In my endeavors to completely fulfill the requirements of this time
honored Station, I have become acutely aware of the great distances which
separate our several Constituent Lodges. We have, this year, traveled
115,000 miles by air; 18,600 by car; 1,600 by bus; 30 miles by subway; 5
miles by cablecar; and 50 yards by camel!
We had qualified for and received the P.S.A. 20,000 mile Honorary
Flight Captain Award in the first three months of our term.
In all of our many visits to the Constituent Lodges we have observed
that for the most part, our Temples and meeting places are in good condition, well kept, and properly maintained. I feel that Masonry is projecting a favorable image within the communities.

We note that many of the Lodges are still experiencing difficulty in filling
the Officers' chairs each year, but there are some very hopeful signs that
this situation may be easing in some areas.
The new Grand Lodge Committee on Sojourners, which is chaired by
Brother Norman Passur and manned by the wonderful brothers of the
International Order of High Twelve, has been hard at work since its official
appointment last October. Their purpose is to identify and encourage sojourning Brothers to attend and affiliate with California Lodges. It is most
pleasing to note that their efforts are already producing the desired result
in increased attendance in many of our Lodges. We are grateful indeed for
the assistance of these fine High Twelve Masons, and this is only one
example of the splendid cooperation which we have received all year from
the several concordant and affiliate bodies of Masonry. The response to
~emphasis upon Unity, within and outside of our Jurisdiction, has been
phenomenal-far beyond our expectations! The warm and gracious hospitality, together with a spirit of total cooperation accorded us everywhere
has reflected the depth and strength of that Unity!
This is not to say we have no problems. Like death and taxes, problems
will always be with us. This year has been no exception. However, through
the pervasive spirit of friendly cooperation which has been the constant,
basic element of Unity, we have been able to resolve most all of our
problems in a mutually satisfactory fashion in the interest of Family Unity.
The one big unsolved problem affecting California Masonry today is the
very same problem which plagues practically every other Grand Jurisdiction in North America: declining membership-and it is a very real problem indeed. It is not, however, without solution. On the contrary, events
of this year have proven conclusively that membership decline can be
stopped completely if we will only apply ourselves to the task.
Among the first things we need to do is to convince the "eternal optimists" within the Fraternity that we REALLY DO HAVE A PROBLEM!
We' are quite literally, "dying off," and we're doing it at the very constant
rate of 5,500 members per year; and incidentally, that figure has remained
constant within two percent for the past fifteen years. To just "break even,"
we must bring in at least 5,500 new members each year. You will notice
that I'said, "BRING IN," because the simple truth is, "THEY ARE NOT
COMING TO US!" Now just before anyone gets his blood-pressure up,
let me state very clearly that I am NOT advocating any solicitation of
members, but there are many excellent ways of bringing worthy, qualified
men into Masonry without asking them to join.
Our wonderful Layman's Night Program; the marvelous Hiram Award
Program; the entertaining Mariners Night Program; and, if we ever get
around to it, a good well-formed program of public relations by the Grand
Lodge of California which will inform the uninitiated that Masonry is a
non-secret organization dedicated to the enlightenment and betterment of
good men and which will also inform them that they must seek Masonic
membership of their own free will and accord. I will have more to say on
this subject later in this message.
Our Layman's Night Program continues to amaze and delight Masters

25

26

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

who have used it in their Lodge. It is the one Grand Lodge Program that
can claim 100 percent success, and it has proven itself absolutely invaluable
as a vehicle for the education of non-Masons and Masons alike. Those
Masters who have not used this valuable tool are penalizing their own
Lodge. I hope that they will soon see the error of their ways and plan at
least one Layman's Night Program each year in their Lodge. I can personally guarantee that the results will be most pleasing, both in terms of more
knowledgeable and interested members, and in terms of new applicants
for the degrees of Masonry in their Lodge.
The Hiram Award Program has been in existence for less than three
years, but its benefits are already quite evident. This award, which was
originally intended for presentation only to non-Past Masters has proven
to be an excellent way for a Lodge to honor its members who have given
service above and beyond the usual call of Masonic duty, but who have
gone thus far unrecognized.
Several Masters who have presented a Hiram Award to one of their
members have reported the receipt of applications for the degrees from
friends or relatives of the recipient who were impressed with the ceremony
and the friendliness of Masonry. The Hiram Award is a great boon to
Masonry, and we are grateful to Brother Walter Kemmerer for bringing it
to the Grand Lodge for the benefit of the several Lodges of this Jurisdiction.
These programs, together with the new Masonic Light Award, which, if
one can judge from the thousands of yellow participation cards that were
returned from the Brethren all over the State, proved to be even more
effective than we had hoped for. I commend all the Brethren who participated in this program and whose names will soon ·grace the pages of our
California Freemason-many of whom will be presented the beautiful Masonic Light Certificate right here at this Grand Lodge Communication.
All of this activity, together with the spirit of Masonic Unity which has
grown so splendidly this year accounts for the atmosphere of progress which
permeates the entire Jurisdiction at this time, and which is characterized
by the many positive comments I have received all over the State in the
past five months; comments such as those which were given me in May at
the Grand Master's barbeque in Fallbrook by the Master of Vista Lodge
No. 687, Worshipful Ernest Fully, Jr. He said, "Grand Master, my Lodge
has in the last three months received 17 applications for the degrees from
men who are in the 23 to 28 year age bracket." When asked what he considered the reason for this, he stated, "I think it is due in a large part to
the cooperation we are receiving this year from the concordant bodies of
Masonry who also meet in our Temple. Not only are they supporting all of
our social events at the Lodge, they are really working hard to bring new
members into Masonry in our area." Brother Fully says that in his opinion,
"The Unity theme is really working," and if 17 new Candidates for the

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

27

degrees of Masonry in Vista Lodge is the yardstick of measurement, then
I think I would have to agree!
Now if this comment from Brother Fully were just an isolated or individual one, I would not be overly impressed, but it is not. In the past four
months I have received like reports from Masters all over the State; positive reports; reports of participation and new growth; reports of coming
together as brothers and Masons, and working together for the betterment
of Masonry. One month ago we were in the "Superior California" region,
around Oroville, Chico, and Paradise to celebrate the 125th Anniversary
of Oroville Lodge No. 103, a reception for the Grand Master in Chico
Lodge No. 111 , and the Institution of the new Alta California Research
Lodge in Paradise. While there, the Master of Chico Lodge reported that
his Lodge had received practically no applications for at least three years,
but they have already received 17 this year. He says that the Layman's
Night Program is really bringing in a fine group of new, young, and interested men to his Lodge. The Master of Oroville Lodge No. 103, Worshipful
Tom Masteller, told me that his Lodge was working on 12 new Candidates
this year, the first in several years. I asked Tom to what he attributed this
new growth and he said, "Well, we've been listening to you say that it's
okay to talk about Masonry with non-Masons, and to tell them what it's
all about, and we've started doing just that. That's how it's happening."
The Master of Molino Lodge No. 150, Worshipful James Lane, told me
that his Lodge had received several new applications this year for just
about the same reasons. Even more recently, at the celebration of the 75th
Anniversary of Mizpah Lodge No. 378 in San Fernando, Worshipful Bruce
Carmitchel, Master of that Lodge reported to me and the Senior Grand
Warden that Mizpah Lodge had received NO applications for the past four
or five years, yet this year they had already received 12, and these from
young men. He said that his Lodge was being greatly assisted by the
affiliate bodies of Masonry; the York Rite, Scottish Rite, and the Shrine.
This report was echoed by the Masters of eleven Lodges in the area around
the Mother Lode country. The Senior Warden of Fresno Lodge No. 247
reported that in the past several years his Lodge had received on the
average of two or three applications per year, but this year they have
received nearly five times that number. And so it goes, o~ and on. The
spirit of Unity is present all over the California Jurisdiction. The feeling
seems to be, "We've sat long enough-now let's be up and doing ....
Let's start building Freemasonry here in California!"
Well, that's the good, now for the bad! It is always good to receive
encouraging reports like those I have just given you. It is at least an·
Indication that we are on the right track in our battle against declining
thembership. Trouble is, we're not doing nearly enough to correct the
problem yet; nor will we be until all the Lodges in the State begin making
use of the many Grand Lodge programs of information and participation,
and when our members really begin to talk about Masonry with the many
fine young men who would seek membership in the Fraternity if only they
knew how to go about it!

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

My Brethren, modern society is challenging us to devise innovative solutions. Apathy and complacency are two insidious enemies! They CAN
be defeated if we launch a determined and effective attack . In most cases
it will test the ingenuity of the Lodge Officers. Regardless of what anyone
else may say, our declining membership is a symptom of a grave malaise.
It needs to be attacked-VICIOUSLY! Our Fraternity faces no external
enemy or forces which inhibit growth! The problem lies WITHIN us! It
is created and perpetuated BY us! It continues to bedevil us because we
have thus far been unwilling to study the facts , to analyze the problems ,
and to devise appropriate solutions. Part of it is due to over-restrictive
regulation , but most of it is due to our unwillingness to recognize the
changes ABOUT us, and to effect changes WITHIN us!
The opportunity is ours my Brothers! We have all the tools necessary
to lift Masonry out of its rut, and we all know that a rut is simply a grave
with both ends kicked out! The challenge is here and now! What a tragedy
it would be if we were to lose by default! But lose we will my Brothers,
if we are not willing to try some new solutions to solve old problems.
We all know that Masonry is.a beautiful living thing, a way of life to be
shared with others, not an ancient relic to be placed on a shelf and guarded
against outsiders. From all appearances the ball is rolling now. The question is, which way do we go-forward, or back? The answer is in your
hands my Brothers!
We are told by many of our older and more experienced leaders not to
worry about our constant membership loss. They say that it is only a
temporary condition-a plateau from which we will rebound again. "It has
happened before, it will happen again." I refuse to accept this! The Grand
Lodge statistics do not support this "plateau view." The fact that in 1981
we have struck the nadir of 1949 tells us, loud and clear, that the so called
"temporary plateau" has spanned 32 years! That's right! We have regressed
in membership from a high of244,586 members in 1965 , to a low of 193,134
this year, almost exactly what our total membership was in the year 1949.
We have gone backward over a 32 year period!
Telling ourselves that we must educate our members, make them better
men and Masons is excellent! Like the old saying, "The operation was a
success, but the patient died," we face a similar problem. As our members
grow older and better educated, they die as "educated Masons," with no
replacements for them! Attrition can be combatted only by bringing in
new members! When the farmer wants to expand his farm, he knows that
he has to till more soiJ_:he has to plow additional land to make it productive. By the same token , we must go OUTSIDE of our ranks to cultivate new contacts if we are to expand our membership and compensate
for our losses. Accordingly, I offer the following recommendation:

the capability shall carry on such a program each year .. For those Lodges
lacking such capability, suitable assistance shall be provided by Grand
Lodge through its Inspectors, Research Lodges, talented speakers, and
duly qualified teachers. Our Layman's Night Programs are an excellent
medium, but they are not being used to their full potential. As a part of
this recommendation, I suggest that a Grand Lodge Committee be appointed to create and implement an effective program. There is absolutely
no reason why we cannot tell the public about our great fraternity! Except
for a few esoteric items, there is a great deal of material in our ritual which
can and should be discussed with non-Masons. The Warden's Workshop
has pointed the way for our Lodge Officers. Now, a program should be
devised to reach the rank and file of our membership, while directing its
major emphasis to the untapped source, the non-Mason!
.Before submitting my second recommendation, I want you all to look
with me to the future of our great Fraternity. I ask you to fall in with the
trend of our day, not because I say so, but because of our problems; our
needs; the urgency for some viable, pragmatic, and realistic solutions. I
ask you to take our collective heads out of the sand, to look around us,
and to devise some means of reducing the seriousness of what we see.
We are all aware of the languor which still pervades many of our Lodges;
the diminishing memberships, the unwillingness of many to assume the
respon.sibi~ities of leadership. We know also of the large number of Lodge
consohdat1ons, the average age of our members, the widespread use of
Past Masters to serve again and again in the various offices of their respective Lodges , and we recognize all of these conditions as blatant testimony to the fact that times are changing, situations are arising which
demand answers, new problems are calling for new solutions.
Our National Government has been suffering comparable difficulties.
A new Presi~ent was elected and inaugurated recently, overcoming all
odds by the simple plea, "Get the Government off our backs!" Since his
election, he has tried desperately to accomplish his objectives. He has
~on-again, against all odds--a drastically reduced budget, tax cuts, and
mcreased defense expenditures. How has he been able to do all this?
Surely, he could not do it alone!
His victories have been accomplished by sensing the mood of the people
~nd capitalizing upon it. He has recognized the burd~ns of over regulation,
its pernicious effects of restrictiveness and strangulation!
~imilarly, I call your attention to the comparable effects of over regul?hon upon our great Fraternity. I speak specifically of our highly restrictive regulations pertaining to advertising! I am well aware of, and completely sympathetic with, the thinking that produced these restrictions.
O~r forebearers had but one objective-a truly commendable one-in
mmd when they adopted these regulations: namely, the welfare of Freemasonry in California and Hawaii.
Since those days, however, there has been a tremendously increased
~mpetition for the dollar, with a remarkably decreased value in the dollar
Itself. People, families, and even organizations-Masonic and nonMasonic-are finding it harder and harder to acquire the dollars and,

consequently, are becoming more and more discriminatory in spending

Recognizing this, other well established and well respected Masonic
Jurisdictions-notably, Utah, Rhode Island, Ohio, Indiana, and New
York, to name a few-have found it expedient to relax their restrictions
upon advertising-WITHOUT LOSS OF RESPECT OR STATURE!
Any advertising firm or business executive will tell you that advertising
is not evil in itself, but rather it is what you say and how you say it that
constitutes the basic determinant of acceptability. Our Brethren in other
Jurisdictions have clearly demonstrated that a truthful, dignified, conservative advertisement that is presented in good taste is an asset to the
Fraternity. It need not be flamboyant, gaudy, or screaming in its appeal;
·
it need not stress the profit or self-aggrandizement motive.
There can be no denying that for too long we have hidden our virtues,
our goals, and our organization behind a self-imposed, restrictive shield.
In so doing, we have created an ogre, a "Masonic Mystique." Librarians
and authors continue to characterize us as a "Secret Society," even though
it is obvious that we are NOT secret. Efforts to correct this unfair categorization and to educate the librarians and others have failed!-Iargely
due to our regrettable shroud of secrecy and reluctance to speak out.
We expect attractive, capable, and worthy men to knock at our doors
and apply for membership with virtually no knowledge about us. Because
we make so little about us known to the uninitiated, we fail to attract
many intelligent, potentially valuable men who have been accustomed to
asking, "Why"-"What for?"
The sports pages often report that today's coaches are confronted with
a new breed of athlete-Players who ask, "Why?" The successful coaches
have been forced to become more flexible, relaxed, responsive, and understanding of the questioning athlete. They have had to learn to yield to
all the inquisitiveness. In many cases, it has made better coaches of them,
compelling them to justify the new plays, assignments, and innovative
formations. And that is not all bad! Times are changing, so are people! If
we are to survive, we too must change to meet the challenges of the day!
With this thought in mind, I respectfully urge you to recognize that our
overly restrictive regulations on advertising MUST be relaxed. As you
know, our Jurisdiction permits limited advertising by DeMolay, Eastern
Star, Scottish and York Rite Bodies, and the Shrine. Such advertising has
expanded and enhanced our public relations, as well as produced much
needed revenues and financial assistance for our related bodies and their
respective charities.

Z072(a) and 2072(b) be deleted and that the first paragraph of Section 1
on Advertising and the first sentence of Section 2 on Public Support in the
Appendix be deleted and repealed.
As an example of what I would consider to be acceptable advertising
under this recommendation, I submit copies of the Masonic publication of
the Grand Lodge of Utah, "The Utah Mason," and the official paper of
the Grand Lodge of Rhode Island, "The Rhode Island Freemason." I find
nothing offensive in either.
There is still another area which needs your consideration. As many of
you know, last March a large group of California Masons, their wives and
families, enplaned at the Los Angeles and the San Francisco airports for
a delightful, highly successful, and richly rewarding Grand Master's pilpage to the Holy Land. The entire project was financially self-sufficient,
without involving one cent of Grand Lodge funds! Those who went were
unanimous in their enthusiastic praise of the trip! New and lasting friendships were made, not only among the tour members, but also with our
guides and many others encountered along the way. While in Israel, most
of the Masons in our group affiliated with the Holy Land Lodge No. 50
in Tel Aviv. The officers of that Lodge are the Grand Lodge Officers of
Israel. This delightful ceremony, and the sumptuous banquet staged by the
Grand Lodge of Israel proved to be exciting highlights of the trip, and
txemplified our Grand Lodge theme, "Freemasonry, an Instrument of
Unity." The feelings of warmth, friendliness, and unanimity were both
ratifying and universal.
In Israel, we followed the tortuous Via Dolorosa, watched the Jews in
solemn prayer at the West, or Wailing Wall, stood on the site of King
Solomon's Temple, took pictures of Mount Moriah and several of the
famous gates to the old Walled City of Jerusalum-especially, the Lions
Gate and the Jaffa Gate. We walked through the Church of the Holy
Sepulchre, and we marveled at the colorful golden domed Mosque that
enshrines the hollow rock, said to be the site of the fabled Sanctum Sanctorum, the spot most highly revered by Jew, Christian, and Moslem.
We climbed by funicular cable car to the top of Massada, the mountain
fortress where 966 Jews defied the Roman legions, then committed mass
suicide rather than fall into Roman slavery. We relived much of the Biblical
history upon which a large portion of our Masonic Ritual is predicated ....
Then, we followed this memorable experience with a few days in Greece
where we recalled our high school lessons in Greek mythology.
By virtue of traveling as a group, and through the excellent planning
and know-how of our Grand Tiler, Worshipful Vic Carbone, we were able
to take this trip for just about one-half the price one would pay if traveling
alone to the same place; and if that were not enough, the bank account
in which the money was kept prepatory to its transmittal to the travel agent
yielded the sum of eleven hundred and some odd dollars interest which
was donated to the Masonic Homes of California in the name of all those
who traveled with the Grand Master to Israel and Greece. The success of
this wonderful pilgrimage proves the feasibility of such Grand Lodge sponsored trips for the enjoyment of the Brethren and their families.

THE GRAND LODGE OF ALASKA

DECISIONS
Number I.
I was asked by a Past Master of a Sacramento Lodge who is also the
Chairman of a DeMolay Advisory Council, if a Lodge which sponsors a
DeMolay Chapter has the authority to expend its funds to pay the two
dollar registration fee for the advisors to the Chapter.
Section 2322, 2nd paragraph of the CMC states, "the following expenditures, among others, shall be deemed to be for the promotion of Fraternal intercourse; contributions to Masonically affiliated Youth organizations, etc ...." I can think of no finer "contribution" to the welfare of our
Masonically affiliated Youth Groups than that of providing the services of
qualified Masons to serve as advisors to the various youth organizations.
I interpret the word "contribution" to mean services as well as dollars,
and if through payment of the two dollar Advisor's Registration fee we are
able to persuade our members to serve the Youth Organizations, then I
believe the expenditure is more than justified. My decision was that the
Lodges are authorized to pay the two dollar Advisor's Registration fee
from their funds.
Number 2.
On yet another occasion, I received a letter from a Lodge in the Southland requesting my approval of their proposal to operate a fireworks stand
in their city, at which sales of commercial fireworks would be made to the
public, the proceeds of such sales to go to the Lodge's Masonic Temple
Association. The Lodge stated in their request that neither the Lodge nor
the Temple Association would be identified with the sale of the fireworks.
My investigation of the proposal revealed that the Lodge and the Temple
Association would be identified with the sale of fireworks due to the legal
requirement that a public sales permit be obtained in the name of the
sponsoring organization, which permit must be visibly displayed at the

On the first weekend of February this year, representatives of twelve of
the nineteen Masonic Lodges of Alaska met in Constitutional Convention
in Anchorage and formed the new Grand Lodge of Alaska. The seven
remaining Alaska Lodges opted to remain with the Grand Lodge of Washington, thereby splitting the state. Recognition was granted this new Grand
Lodge almost immediately by at least three other Grand Lodges, but not
by Washington. Because of this, I found it necessary to inform all California Lodges that the twelve Lodges which formed the new Grand Lodge
of Alaska were not recognized by us, and no fraternal intercourse could
be carried on between them and Lodges of the California Grand Lodge.
This presented some real problems to those California members who held
dual membership in one or more of the unrecognized Alaska Lodges.
I instructed the Committee on Recognition of Foreign Grand Lodges to
study the formation of the Alaska Grand Lodge and report their findings
as soon as possible. We then awaited further action by the Grand Lodge
of Washington before making any further decisions in this regard. At the
Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Washington, official recognition was granted to the Grand Lodge of Alaska with the provision
that the seven holdout Lodges could remain under the jurisdiction of
Washington. The Grand Master of Alaska was present at that session and
voiced the approval of his Grand Lodge for the action taken, including the
seven Lodges remaining in the Grand Lodge of Washington. I received the
report of our Committee on Recognition of Foreign Grand Lodges late.in
June. They recommended that we recognize the Alaska Grand Lodge.
J1.ecognizing a need to alleviate the problem precipitated by declaring the
twelve Alaska Lodges unrecognized, or irregular, I exercised the authority
granted me under Section 300 of the California Masonic Code, and granted
official recognition to the Grand Lodge of Alaska, subject to the approval
of this Grand Lodge at this Annual Communication. A proper motion to
this effect will be presented for your consideration at a later time in these
ptocedings.

In mid-February, in the company of Deputy Grand Master Robert 0.

pleased and honored at being asked to prepare and deliver one of the four

"Publicity and Public Relations, the Proper Use Thereof." This proved an
excellent opportunity to stress the extreme importance of publicizing ~he
activities of Masonry, and for establishing and carrying on a comprehensive
program of public relations within our communities and to non-Masons.

Germaine to the Conference of Grand Masters, I must report to you the
following: In a meeting of nine Grand Masters of Jurisdictions surrounding
California, which was held in Salt Lake City, Utah, grave concern was
voiced by all present regarding the value of attendance at the Grand Masters' Conference. The concensus was that some attempt should be made
to increase the effectiveness of the Conference. As spokesman for those
nine Grand Masters, I presented to the Grand Masters' Conference .in
Orlando, a resolution that a committee be appointed to study the entire
structure of the Conference and recommend possible changes to make the
Conference worthwhile and productive.
That resolution was unanimously approved by all the Grand Masters of
North America and the committee thus appointed consisted of the Grand
Masters of Utah, Florida, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, and California. We
are now pursuing that study, the results of which will be reported to t~e
Conference of Grand Masters for their action when they next meet m
February 1982 in Washington, D.C.

Knowing that most of us are goal oriented, we decided this year to raise
our sights in an attempt to match endowment fund contributions to the
spiralling rate of inflation. Our goal this year was set at 1.5 million, and
darned if we didn't almost make it! Thanks to the devoted efforts of Chairman Bob Hilts, the hard work of all members of the Endowment Board,
and the generosity of the wonderful Masons of California, the total this
year was well in advance of one and one-quarter million dollars! My Brethren, you may all be rightly proud of yourselves for this splendid accomplishment!
A fresh new approach was applied to our public schools program this
year, and the results were most gratifying. At the suggestion of Past Grand
Master Eugene S. Hopp, we adopted the concept of "Total Community
Commitment!" This concept received the immediate approval and support
of the California State School Board Association through its president,
Sheldon Baker, and the executive secretary, Herb Salinger. Invitations
were extended to the president of each school board in California to address the stated meetings of all Lodges, and in each case these meetings
provided new, constructive information about public education and developed some fresh new approaches to many of the problems which face
our public schools today. The large number of positive comments and
letters from all over the state bear testimony to the effectiveness of "Total
Community Commitment" in free public education.
We are most grateful to Sovereign Grand Commander Henry C. Clausen
for the cooperation of the Scottish Rite who contributed $7 ,000 to assist
in the free distribution of school book covers to over 100,000 students this
year. Freemasonry and free public education make excellent allies!
We are also grateful to all members of the Grand Lodge Committee on
Information and Responsibility for their excellent program this year.
Equipped with some brand new, interesting and informative information,
they have held seminars all over the state and in Hawaii for the purpose
of educating our members. Reports have it that they succeeded admirably
well!

me, this is the way I would hope it might be:

As you would have wished me to do.
Our work was good for you and for me,
And so shall I remember you.

"ADVERTISIN G AND SOLICITING THE GENERAL PUBLIC.
The Masonic Youth Orders and other Masonic organizations as defined in
the Commercialism Regulations relating to adult orders in the Appendix
hereof, may advertise and solicit the general public for fund raising activities within the bounds of propriety and provided that fair prices are
charged."
RESOLVED FURTHER, that the first paragraph of Section 2072 of
the California Masonic Code and the first paragraph of the advertising
portion of the regulations governing organizations subject to the jurisdiction of the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California in the
Appendix of the California Masonic Code be amended to each read as
follows:
"No Lodge, or member of a Lodge, shall solicit, sponsor, insert, place
or print advertising of any kind in or for any medium or publication, which
purports to be Masonic in name or character, unless such medium or publication is recognized by Grand Lodge as Masonic."
RESOLVED FURTHER, that Annotations 2072(a) and 2072(b) be deleted.
RESOLVED FURTHER, that Annotation 2072(a) be repeated in full
as Annotation 2072(a) after eliminating the words "without advertising"
and "Clausen, G.M. 1955, pp. 61, 355" and that the following be added:
"Juris. Com. 1981, p. - - · "
To place the matter before Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of the
Resolution.

RECOMMENDA TION No. 1

PROGRAM OF MASONIC EDUCATION FOR NON-MASONS

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The ~rand ~aster recommends "a well-planned, aggressive program of
Masomc education for non-Masons." As a part of his Recommendati on he
suggests that a Grand Lodge Committee be appointed "to create and implement an effective program."
There is nothing inconsistent with the policy and general purposes of
the Grand Lodge when information about Masonry is conveyed to nonMasons with dignity and with certain limitations.
As to the suggestion that a Committee be appointed, if the incoming
Grand Master finds no present Committee is suitable for the creation of
such a program, he has authority to appoint a special committee for that
purpose (CMC 1250). However, we assume that implementation of such
a program would be commenced only after the program has been created
by the Committee and approved by the Grand Lodge.
We recommend a "Yes" vote with the understanding that a new Committee may not be needed and that implementation would require Grand
Lodge approval after its creation.
The Committee on Ritual:
The Committee on Ritual concurred in the report of the Policy and
·
General Purposes Committee.
Committee on Masonic Information and Responsibility:
No report presented.
The Grand Master's Recommendation was Adopted.
RECOMMENDAT ION No. 2

ADVERTISIN G IN MASONIC PUBLICATIONS

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence to which the Grand Master's Recommendation No. 2 has been referred reports as follows:
The Grand Master, to parallel the practice of many other Grand Jurisdictions which allow advertising, has recommended that advertising be
permitted, provided that no pressure is brought to bear to sell such advertising and that it be within the bounds of propriety.
To carry out the intent of the Grand Master, your Committee submits
the following legislation:
RESOLVED, that Section 2071 of the California Masonic Code be
amended to read as follows:

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The Grand Master's Recommendation No. 2 is, first, that advertising in
Masonic publications be permitted, provided no pressure is brought to
bear to sell such advertising, and, secondly, that Section 2071 CMC, now
applying to Masonic Youth Orders only, be amended so that Lodges and
concordant bodies "may advertise and solicit the general public for fund
raising activities within the bounds of propriety and that fair prices are
charged" (Section 2071, CMC).
It is recognized that advertising in Shrine-sponsored football games is
permitted under Section 2072 CMC, but such advertising is strictly limited
to "charity football game programs only sponsored by organizations requiring Masonic membership as a prerequisite for membership therein,
when the proceeds of the game go to a Masonic or Masonic-related
charity"... and, further, "that the proceeds from such advertisements shall
not exceed the cost of printing and mailing or distributing such programs ...."
Public respect of our Lodges and this Grand Lodge has been enhanced
by our regulations prohibiting commercial ventures and the solicitation of
advertising from the public. Few today remember the abuses of those times
many years ago when we did not have our present regulations.
Allowing advertising will create pressures, subtle and not so subtle, upon
advertisers no matter how clear our present intent may be, and we will
lose an important base of respect for Freemasonry. We now refrain from

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

making demands upon our communities for money; we do not compete
in the commercial world, and we do not allow ourselves to be classified
with the numerous groups which regularly seek funds from the public
through an ever-expanding variety of schemes and methods, including socalled advertising support. The purpose of accepting advertising in our
publications can only be to raise money. Surely it cannot generate good
will; nor increase the respect with which we are held in our communities.
A further and important concern is the possibility of involvement in
lawsuits in the event of rejection of an advertisement, for whatever reason,
and the subsequent charge of discrimination on the part of the would-be
adveJ1iser. Such suits are all too common, and Freemasonry should never
be a defendant in a suit of this sort.
Our present regulations on advertising in no way prevent us from telling
non-Masons about Masonry. Telling the Masonic story should not be confused with allowing advertising as a fund~raising device.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes believes more detriment than benefit would result from the adoption of this proposal, that it
is not needed, and that it would constitute a major policy change for this
Grand Lodge.
'
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends that the
Grand Master's Recommendation No. 2, as presented, be not approved,
and a "No" vote is recommended.

To carry out the intent of the Grand Master, your Committee moves the
approval of the Recommendation and the addition of a new Annotation
numbered 1058a, as follows:
"Grand Lodge approved a policy whereby Grand Masters may arrange
and sponsor a trip, provided that such trip would be self-sustaining, with
no involvement of Grand Lodge funds, and that all arrangements and
advertising of such trips be of a nature befitting the dignity and keeping
of this Grand Lodge."
Since neither the Grand Master's Recommendation nor this motion
amends the law of the Grand Lodge, only a majority vote is required for
adoption.

RECOMMENDATION No. 3

POLICY TO PERMIT GRAND MASTER
TO ARRANGE AND SPONSOR TRIPS

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to which the Grand Master's Recommendation No. 3 has been referred, reports as follows:
The Grand Master has recommended that Grand Lodge establish policy
which would permit furure Grand Masters to arrange and sponsor selfsupporting trips.

43

The Corµmittee on Policy and General Purposes:
Grand Master's Recommendation No. 3 recommends, "That policy be
established by the vote of this Grand Lodge which would permit any future
Grand Master to arrange and sponsor a trip, provided that such trip would
be self-sustaining with no involvement of Grand Lodge funds, etc."
In 1976 Grand Master Roberts presented his Recommendation No. 2
titled "Travel Tours-Grand Lodge to Sponsor." The report of your Committee on Policy and General Purposes reported, "It is the opinion of the
Committee that the Grand Lodge of California should not be connected
with any commercial activity." That opinion was upheld by the Grand
Lodge and the Grand Master's Recommendation was not approved.
Grand Master Lemons' Recommendation No. 2 states, "Our trip this
year has established that such activity is possible at no risk to the Grand
Lodge." To the contrary, your Committee on Policy and General Purposes
believes that there are indeed risks involved to your Grand Lodge.
Whenever the Grand Lodge of California sponsors a trip it is exposed
to the responsibility of liability insurance and safety of those traveling on
trips. There could be grave consequences to your Grand Lodge in the
event of air disasters, injury, taking of hostages, or other events which
could result in legal actions being taken against Grand Lodge, ending in
financial disaster.
This Recommendation is fraught with grave responsibilities and for the
future security of the Grand Lodge of California.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes states that this type
of activity is not consistent with the long established policies and general
purposes of this Grand Lodge and recommends that Grand Master's Recommendation No. 3 be not approved.

The Committee on Commercialism:
No report presented. (see report on Recommendation No. 2)
The Grand Master's Recommendation was Adopted.

DECISION No. 1

In fact, the three sections mentioned (2318, 2320 and 2322) are the
authority for a Lodge's expenditure of funds. Expenditures not expressly
authorized by these Sections are not allowed. For example, a salary for a
Lodge Treasurer has been held to be improper (CMC Section 2320b). A
Lodge may not pay a monthly pension to a Past Master who has served
for many years as Secretary (Section 2320d). A Master cannot be paid a
fee for conducting a funeral service (Section 2906b). In each such case the
payment would encourage someone to again render similar service. There
no more authority for such pay when the service is rendered to an
affiliated youth organization.
A long established policy of this Grand Lodge would be overturned if
this Decision were allowed to stand.
We recommend a "No" vote.

REGISTRATION FEE OF MASONIC ADVISORS
TO DeMOLAY CHAPTER
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to which the Grand Master's Decision No. 1 has been referred, reports as follows:
The Grand Master has properly determined that Section 2322 of the
California Masonic Code, which permits Lodge contributions to Masonically affiliated youth organizations, authorizes a Lodge to pay the registration fee of Masonic advisors to a Chapter of DeMolay.
We move the approval of the Decision and the addition of a new Annotation numbered 2322 I as follows:
"A Lodge may pay the registration fee of a Masonic advisor to a Chapter
of the Order of deMolay."
Since neither the Grand Master's Decision No. 1 nor this motion amends
the law of the Grand Lodge, only a majority vote is required for adoption.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The Grand Master's Decision No. 1 authorizes a Lodge to pay from its
funds the two dollar ($2.00) registration fee required of an advisor to a
DeMolay Chapter.
As the Grand Master noted, CMC Section 2322 provides that contributions to Masonically affiliated youth organizations are proper expenditures for the social purpose of "the promotion of fraternal intercourse."
Thus the contributions of money to affiliated youth orders is a proper way
of providing assistance to such organizations.
The problem here is that when the Lodge pays the two dollar ($2.00)
registration fee for an advisor to a DeMolay Chapter it is not contributing
money to the Chapter; instead it is paying a registration fee paid by the
Mason who is the advisor.
The Grand Master reasons that our Lodge contributions need to be of
personal service as well as money, that the payment of the fee encourages
such service. However, Section 2322 is the third in a series of Sections
which authorize expenditures of money (2318 for required program, 2320
discretionary expenditures, and 2322 for social purposes).
The question then is whether the Lodge is authorized to pay on behalf
of a member an expense which he incurs in contributing his time to a
Masonically affiliated youth group.
A first impression is that the amount is so small and the need for encouraging the service so great that there must be some way to justify such
a payment. The vice of that thinking is that upon the same reasoning a
Lodge could pay a Brother to serve as Advisor. If it becomes difficult to
find someone to serve in that capacity some Lodge some place some time
could properly reason from this Decision that an expenditure for such
purpose was proper. It would not be.

45

•s

The Committee on Youth Orders:
The Youth Orders Committee, as you might expect, is in favor of anything which would encourage the support of our Youth Orders by our
Lodges and their members. However, we know those motivations come
from the heart and not the head.
We are somewhat dismayed that a $2.00 fee should be the issue around
which such a decision is made.
However, if in any Lodge at any time, it seems proper to encourage
such support by the payment of this fee, we would be in favor of it, and
recommend a "Yes" vote.
The Grand Master's Decision was approved.

PROCLAMATION
PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK - 1981
"PUBLIC SCHOOLS: AMERICA'S RICHEST RESOURCE"
America has been richly blessed with abundant resources for which
we are indeed grateful. The value of a resource is usually measured
by ~he amount of wealth which it produces. By this same standard, our
public Schools are AMERICA'S RICHEST RESOURCE, for they have produced
riches far beyond any calculation.
Fo~ more than 200 years our Public Schools have produced generations of well-informed citizens whose love of liberty, whose dedication
to the principles of democracy, and whose scholastic attainments have
created the most affluent society on earth.
Our Public Schools, like all other resources, must be treasured
and preserved if they are to continue yielding comparable dividends
in the years to come.
Records show that many of America's resources are being rapidly
depleted. This must never happen to our Public Schools! To provide
for a free and enlightened citizenry - to preserve our system of
Democracy - to keep our Nation strong and retain the bounties which
we all enjoy today, our concept of free public education for the youth
of America must be vigorously and continuously supported. TOTAL
COMMUNITY COMMI'l'TMENT is required!
That these objectives may be promoted and advanced, I do now
proclaim
PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK during APRIL, 1981
throughout California and Hawaii, and I call upon all Masonic LOdges
to arrange with the schools in their area for a mutually acceptable
week in the Month of APRIL to be set aside for the observance of this
event with appropriate ceremonies and programs.
Furthermore, I direct that no LOdge Programs or Meetings, other
than the Stated Meetings, beheld during the designated week which might
conflict with Public Schools Observances: and
That this Proclamation be read at the April Stated Meeting of all
J,odges and, where feasible, that it also be published in LOdge bulletins

PROCLAMATION
PROCIAMATION
YOUTH ACTIVITIES MONTH
TO:

MARCH, 1981

All Masonic Lodges in California and Hawaii
What the youth of today need, more
than anything else, is a good model,
not a critic.

our Order has long ago realized and promoted the benefit of
preserving our tomorrow through the youth of today. There is no
finer example of tomorrow than the young people who populate our
fine youth orders--Job's Daughters, Rainbow for Girls and the
Order of DeMolay.
It is my sincere hope that each Lodge is already heartily
engaged in a wide and varied program of mutual cooperation with
and support for the fine youth groups in your area. In such a
relationship, you will discover the benefits are mutual and immediate. These fine young people offer a measure of youthful talent
and enthusiasm to add success to any of your activities. They
come to you with full admiration and respect which you need only
to return in order to preserve.
I, therefore, proclaim the month of March to be Youth Activities
Month in California and Hawaii. I encourage and urge each Lodge to
schedule special activities in recognition of and support for these
youth groups--not as the total extent of your support for them during the year but merely to lend special emphasis to this most
important area of our fraternal lives.
I ask that this communication be read at the March Stated
Meeting and each Lodge to schedule youth activities and recognition
throughout the year as often as is possible.
Fraternally,

II~~~
H. Do~s Lemons
Grand Master

MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT MONTH
In the words of the Prophet, it is writtenr
"Now the end of the Commandment is charity
out of the pure heart, and of a good conscience, and faith unfeigned --- and above
all these things put on charity, which is
·the bond of perfectness. "
In the Holy Writ, the word charity was used to define acts
of hwnan kindness, benevolence, compassion and Good Will. Its
true meaning represented a tenderness of heart and a generosity
of spirit that was born of God's Love.
There is no greater expression of true Brotherly Love than
the voluntary support of the Masonic Homes of California, through
the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund, for this is indeed, the highest
duty of Masons, to aid, support and to protect one another.
In today's morass of the economic chaos, financial support
of our Masonic Homes is more important than ever before. It is
imperative that EVERY Mason in California and Hawaii participate
in this marvelous work of love, ever remembering that it is only
in giving that we receive.
The ~o Masonic Homes of California are monuments to the
generosity and love of our Brethren in california and Hawaii.
They stand as beacons of comfort and security for our elderly
Brethren, their wives and widows at Union city and our wonderful
children at Covina.
I feel confident that all Masons of California and Hawaii
will respond generously in this one great Masonic dgty. It is
directed that this Proclamation be read at the Stated Meeting of
May, 1981 and wherever possible be reprinted in Ledge bulletins or
otherwise distributed to each Ledge member.
Fraternally,

CONSTITT:JTION OBSERVANCE MONTH
At certain intervals in the history of mankind, high points are reached,
wherein men are afforded the opportunity to rise to great heights -- to
meet the challenges of the times, and to produce for their posterity,
certain fundamental and lasting concepts.
History decreed September 17, 1787 to be just such a time, for it was on
that date, during the Revolutionary war era that a small group of patriots1
many of whom were Masons, assembled in Independence Hall in Philadelphia
and produced the great and inspired document which proclaimed a new Nation~
founded that its people might enjoy the blessings of liberty for themselves and their posterity -- THE CONSTITUTION OF THE UNITED STATES OF
AMERICA! It was, and always will be, a modern and living document which
contains such basic, non-controversial and undeniably'true principles
for the regulation and conduct of man, that, if preserved, will forever
secure the dignity and freedom of every American citizen. This is accomplished by the establishment of government-under-law, as opposed to government-by-men, and by securing for each of us certain individual basic
rights under the law.
Today, we are surrounded by those who would destroy the constitution
outright -- or weaken it so that the intent of those who gave us that
immortal doeument would become nullified. As Masons, we must defend our
constitution with all our might and main, and stand firm for the principlet
set forth therein!
Upon entering Independence Hall for the first time, one is inevitably impressed with the admonition, ''Walk Proudly Here, Americans, Amid the s ·,-mbol!
of Your Birthright".
It is in that same spirit that I call upon each Lodge to participate in
activities which may arouse conununity spirit, and insure support of the
Constitution of the United States of America.
I, therefore, proclaim September, 1981 to be Constitution Observance Montht
and direct every Lodge in this Jurisdiction to participate in a suitable
observance of the Anniversary of the signing of the Constitution, such
event to be held as close as possible to the actual Anniversary date of
September 17. I further direct that this Proclamation shall be read
at each Stated Meeting during the Month of August and September, 1981.
Dated:

July 9, 1981
