Grand Master

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The financial statements for our fiscal year ended June 30, 1981, verified
by the firm, Lindquist, von Husen and Joyce of San Francisco, are presented herein.
Your attention is directed, particularly, to a new and expanded form of
presentation of operating and financial data. We can now report to you
that our conversion from "modified cash" to "accrual" accounting has been
completed.
During the past year we have replaced a ten-year-old bookkeeping machine with a mini-computer system; hired sorely needed technically trained
accounting personnel; secured professional appraisals of all properties in
order to provide adequate insurance coverages and to properly reflect (for
the first time) depreciation of all capital assets; and, working closely with
Crocker Bank, have instituted up-to-date methods of cash management.
As a result, our books and records, and resulting statements, now reflect
results consistent with present day accounting principles as prescribed by
the public accounting profession.
Of greater importance, we feel that we are now provided with those
internal controls so necessary to account for and safeguard the total assets
of all Grand Lodge entities, now well in excess of one hundred million
dollars.
My second year as your Grand Treasurer has been one during which I
have experienced a growing appreciation of the time and attention devoted
to a variety of Masonic interests by our Grand Master, Most Worshipful
H. Douglas Lemons and his fellow officers.
Last, but not least, my congratulations to Very Worshipful Robert A.
Klinger in his first year as a very capable Grand Secretary, and my sincere
thanks to his fine staff for their help and assistance.

Respectfully submitted,
JOHN A. SICKENBERGER, Grand Treasurer

Referred to the Committee on Distribution. The Committee on Distribution referred entire report to the Committee on Finance.

ACCOUNTING DEPARTMENT

The Accounting Department of Grand Lodge. which provides accounting and financial reporting services to Grand Lodge and its various entities.
has undergone consideratilc change and redirection over the year just
ended. Jn keeping with adoption of the accrual method of accounting
during the previous year. a new unified Chart of Accounts has tieen implemented. data recordation and summarization procedures have been revised and job responsibilities redefined and grouped so as to provide for
an even distribution of work load coupled with task specialization.
Also during the year. a new computer system became operational for
the systematic tracking of accounting data of the more than 30 funds comprising the Grand Lodge anJ its several entities. This system includes the
atiility to quickly analylc changes in account balances and to provide
budget comparisons for management's information and use.
Finally. our accounting staff has been strengthened through the addition
of several key employees and the training and organization of our remaining staff.

ACTION OF GRAND LODGE

The Masonic ~ri a l Commission found him not guilty of un-Masonic
conduct. When this matter was brought to the attention of the 1980 Annual
Communication of Grand Lodge, the findings were reversed and a new
trial ordered. It was determined by Grand Lodge that Charity Lodge
should file ame~ded charges that specified with clearness and precision the
offense complained of. pursuant to Section 3328. C.M.C.
The new trial was held on April 25, 1981 in the member's absence. The
member had not responded to notifications of the second trial within the
30 day limitation .
At the second trial the member was found guilty of un-Masonic conduct
and the penalty recom mended as Suspension.
Your Committee o~ Trial Review ~elieves the act of attempting to conceal stolen property 1s of such seventy that the penalty should be raised
from Suspension to Expulsion.
RESOLVED, that the findings of the Trial Master be affirmed but the
penalty be raised to Expulsion.

The Committee on Trial Review:
Three years ago. our Chairman Emcritu~ Harold S. Morri-;on suffered
a ~evc rc stroke. One of the most important events in his life each year was
Grand Lodge. He was o ne of the most loyal and effective workers this
Grand Lodge ever had . I am happy to report that last night I spoke on
the telephone with Harold , and he was able to communicate to me his
wish that he were here and his warm greetings to you all.
There have been referred to vour Committee on Trial Review since the
1980 Communic;ation eighteen trial records. two of which arc petitions for
restoration.
Your Committee ha~ reviewed each of Trial Records 2132 . 2153. 2155,
2156. 2157. 2158, 2163. 2164 and 2165 and finds that the proper procedure
was followed in caeh case: that the result is supporteJ by the evidence in
the records of each case: that there wa~ substa ntial compliance with the
procedural requirements of our Constitution and OrJinances; and that
there are no miscarriages of justiee.
Your Committee therefore submits the following Resolution :
RESOLVED, that in each of the above-numbered Trial Records the
judgment and the penalty imposed be and are ratified. affirmed and approved.
TRIAL RECORDS No. 2067 AND 2101
Your Committee has considered petitions for restoration in Trial Record
2067. by a former member of Clayton Valley Lodge No. 756. and Trial
Record 2101. by a former member of Temesrnl Lodge No. 314.
Membership in our Fraternity must be jealously guarded and once membership is lost by an act of un-Masonic conduct. restoration to the rights
and privileges of Freemasonry should be granted only on clear and convi ncing evidence of atonement and rehabilitation .
In Trial Record 2067 the former member has expressions of support
from his form er Lodge and from members of the community. However.
because of the gravity of breach by th e former member of his position of
trust. vour Committee does not feel that sufficient time has elapsed to
allow for the required showing.
In Trial Record 2101. not only has there been insufficient time for the
required showing. but the former member has in no way augmented the
record ·ince Grand Lodge denied his prior petition for restoration.
Your Committee therefore submits the following Resolution :
RESOLVED. that the Petitions for Restoration in Trial records 2067
amJ 2101 be denied.

TRIAL RECORD No. 2154

In t~i s case a member of Smyrna Lodge No. 352 was charged with unMas~nic conduct on the specification that he did willfully. unlawfully, and
feloniously take the property of another of a value exceeding $200.00. a
violatio n of Sectio~ 487, Subd!vision 1, California Penal Code, a felony.
He was sentence~ in the Supenor Court to one year in the county jail anJ
placed on probation. for three year~. the accused having plead guilty. In
response to the notice that Masonic charges were being preferred. the
accused wrote a lttter to th e Master of the Lodge requesting that he he
suspended from the Lodge. The Masonic Trial resulted in a verdict of
guilty and imposed a penalty of Suspension.
Your Committee feels that an offense of this kind is such a serious
violation as to merit a greater penalty than Suspension. We. therefore.
submit the fo llowing resolution:
RESOLVED. that the finding of guilty of un-Masonic conduct he affirmed . and that the penalty be raised to Expulsion.

Charges in this matter were brought against a then member of San
Joaquin Lodge No. 19. They alleged that the Brother was guilty of unMaso nic conduct in that, while driving under the inftue nce of liquor and
drugs. he negligently caused bodily injury to another: in short. felony
drunk driving. The proceedings we re properly conducted . The Tnal Master
found the accused guilty and suspe nded him "for the period of formal
probatio n." In this sentence. the Trial Master was refe rring to the probation term set by California 's St ate Court, five years.
Your Trial Review Committee concur!> with the findings of the Trial
Maste r. but believes that a modification of the sentem:e is clearly indicated.
The California Masonic Code makes no provision for a limited sentence
of suspension. When suspension is proper. it is indete rminate . continuing
until valid restoration upon application . Here, however. thic; Committee
unanimously agreed that the severity of the offense requires Expulsion,
ra ther than Suspension.

RESOLVED, that the finding of guilty of un-Masonic conduct in Trial
Record No. 2161 be aftirmed. and that the penalty be raised to Expulsion.

TRIA L RECORD No. 2 160

This Trial Record involves a member of Paso Robles Lodge No. 286
who was charged with un-Masonic conduct in that. first. he did rece ive
stolen property. second. he committed this offe nse again st a Brother Mason. The accused was a police officer at the time. employed on a part-time
basis by the offended Brother.
The charges, originally brought in 1978. we re ret urned to the Lodge for
amendment as to the wording of the specifications. Rat her than amending,
the charges were withdrawn. In February of 1981. prope rl y pre pared
charges were fi led. Within the prope r time followi ng his receipt of the
charges. the accused responded by letter to the Lodge. The letter indicated
confusion on the part of the accused as to his stat us and the proceedings.
The respo nding letter also asserted that the acc used believed he was not
guilty.
Despite the above, the Trial Master's records rcftect a proceeding without Trial by Commissio n. We can assume the confusion on the part o f the
accused , a misinterpretation of his letter. a change of plea by the accused.
or other valid or invalid possibilities. Such assumptions are not , however.
a permitted luxury: neither are they the proper basis for a penalty as severe
as Expulsion from our Masonic Fraternity.
Your Tri al Review Committee submits the fo llowing resolution:
RESOLVED. that the findings and penalty in Trial Record No. 2160 he
rever ·ed and remanded to Paso Robles Lodge No. 286 for properly conducted and recorded trial proceedings on the same charges.

TRIAL RECORD No. 2102

In Trial Record No. 2162. the accused. a member of Lodge Maui No.
472, was charged with theft of two automobiles from hi~ employer, a
Brother Master Mason.
After trial hy a commission . he was found guilty of each specification
and of the charge of un-Masonic conduct and the penalty was affixed at
Suspension.
Your Committee is concerned that not only was the accused found guilty
of a criminal activity, theft. but in a more basic sense. he wa~ found guilty
of violating hi~ Masonic obligations to a Broth er Master Mason.
Trial procedures appear to have been in order and the evidence was
sufficient to warrant a guilty findin g. However, thi s Co mmittee bcliev~s
that an offense of this nature is such a serious violation of our Masonic

This present meeting of your Trial Review Committee marks the third
occasion on which this matter has been. in one form or another. before
us. There can be, perhaps , no more dramatic indication of the value placed
upon our Masonic affiliations, than this continuing and se rious consideration.
The accused herein was originally charged with un-Masonic conduct in
that he provided pornographic films to a membe r of DeMolay for use at
a high school athletic team party. Although the accused was a member of
Yorba Linda Lodge No. 469. Trial by Commission was had in another
Lodge by o rder of the Grand Master. resulting in a ve rdict of acquittal.
Upon revie w. your Committee agreed that, although the evidence supported the fi ndings that the accused was not guilt y of the charges and

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

specifications as presented. they also disclosed the likelihood of guilt in
that he, having the knowledge and opportunity to prevent delivery and
use of the pornographic films hy the DcMolay, failed to do so. The Grand
Lodge affirmed the acquittal, ordering new charges filed and proceedings
thereon.
The matter was referred by the Grand Master to a second Lodge for
trial and a new Trial ~faster was appointed. Following argument of counsel
for both accused and accuser. the charges were dismissed by the new Trial
Master based upon that Trial Master's belief that the accused had previously been placed in jeopardy. Grand Lodge reversed this action and remanded the matter for trial proceedings.
The accused's own Lodge, Yorba Linda Lodge No. 469, was directed by
the Grand Master to commence these proceedings. A new Trial Master
was appointed. charges were filed and served. Although there is some
question as to when service actually took place and exactly when the response of the accused was received by the Lodge, the facts show that the
response of the accused was received beyond the thirty-day period specified in the California Masonic Code and. further, that the accused had
actual notice no less than two weeks prior to the ter~ination of that period.
The lack of diligence by the accused has contributed greatly to the problems inherent in this matter, as set forth hereafter.
After the lapse of the proper thirty-day notice period, no response from
the accused having been received within that time, the Trial Master proceeded, pursuant to the provisions of California Masonic Code Section
3340, which provides in part ''if, within the time provided for in the notice
hereinbefore in this article specified. the accused shall not have filed in
writing with the Secretary of the Lodge his plea of nor guilty. the Master
of said Lodge or the Trial Master. as the case may be. shall personally
make a complete investigation and shall determine whether the charge
and specifications are true, causing the facts relating thereto to be reduced
to writing. in triplicate; and he shall make a finding as to the guilt or
innocence of the accused, and shall fix the penalty therefor."
As can be seen from the preceding. the Trial Master acted correctlv and
as required by Section 3340. No discretion being provided therei~ for
action upon receipt of an untimely denial, the Trial Master properly proceeded to conduct an investigation. making a finding of guilty of un-Masonic conduct and setting the penalty of Expulsion.
The following is a portion of the Trial Master's findings: "My investigation and examination of the aforementioned record of trial revealed
ample evidence that the accused had knowledge of certain pornographic
films; that a plan existed to show the films to minor young men; and that
the accused failed to make a genuine attempt to prevent the film from
being furnished to a 16 year old DeMolay. The record of trial further
revealed that the accused knowingly facilitated the furnishing of the films
hy his employee and that the accused allowed the film to he picked up at
the accused's home by a 16 year old DeMolay youth."
Although the acts of the Trial Master were both legal and competent,
the accused nonetheless believes himself entitled to trial by a Commission;

11owever. the California Maso nic Code did not afford the Trial Master. nor
docs it afford your Committee. an alternati ve. Based upon the record
before it, and the mandate mentioned, your Committee recommends that
the Trial Master's decision be affirmed.
Your Committee. to afford the Grand Lodge a meaningful opportunit y
to make its determination hereon, first presents the alternatives available
to you under the provisions of the California Masonic Code. Section 3502
of the Code provides that. after the report of the Trial Review Committee
has been presented "the Grand Lodge may affirm. modify. or reve rse the
judgment of the Lodge or make such other order relative thereto as it
shall dee m proper.'' To provide the opportunity stated. alternative resolutions are submitted, the first to affirm the Trial Record and confirm this
Committee's recommendation, the second supporting t he wishes of the
accused , contrary to t he provisions of the Code. vacating the decisions of
the Trial Master and ordering Trial by Commission on the same charges.
Present procedures provide nothing further. The first resolution will be
submitted and voted upon: if necessary, the second will be treated likewise.
Your Committee submits the following resolution:
RESOLVED. that the findings and penalty in Trial Record No. 2102 be
affirmed .

REPORT OF GRAND LECTURER
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Brethren , it is the duty and honor of your Grand Lecturer to submit the
following report in compliance with C.M.C. Section ll 14-4th.
RITUAL CONFERENCES

The Divisional Conferences for Inspectors and Ritual Committee meetings were held as follows:
Divisfon I-February 13-15, in Santa Rosa, conducted by the W. Donald
E. Weisse.
Division II-April 10-12, in Sacramento, conducted by the W. Louis A.
Lasell, Sr.
Division III- March 20-22, in Los Gatos. conducted by the W. Ulysses
G. Patropulos.
Division IV-May 15-17, in Porterville, conducted by the W. Joe Hammond.
Division V-June 19-21, in Oxnard, conducted by the W. Roy J. Henville.
Division VI-January 16-18, in Long Beach, conducted by the W. Morton B. Glick.
In addition to these meetings the Assistant Grand Lecturers and the
Inspectors conducted numerous Seminars for the purpose of exemplifing
the ritual for all interested Brethren. Your Grand Lecturer attended two
of these Seminars. one in San Jose and the other in Sacramento.
RECOMMENDATION BY THE GRAND LECTURER

After extensive Committee discussion and actual witnessing of the Mortgage Burning Ceremony and then having the Ritual Committee practice
the Ceremony as agreed on, it is the unanimous opinion of the Committee
that the following floor movement changes would enable all in attendance
to have an unobstructed view of the actual Ceremony: Each Grand Lodge
Officer would return to his station from the Altar after pouring the contents of his vial into the crucible. The Grand Master would have no change
in his movements as he conducts all of his work at the crucible East of the
same, it being necessary that he remain at that place. This recommendation
is being made as ·a result of the comments of many of the Brethren who
have attended these Ceremonies and have remarked that they were unable
to view the work of the Grand Master and in particular the actual burning
of the mortgage itself.
INSPECTORS AND CONDITION OF LODGES

The Inspectors during the past year have shown a real desire and effort
to improve Masonry in this Jurisdiction . Their support of our Grand Master has been exemplary. The goal set by the Grand Master for the Homes'
Endowment effort was taken as a personal challenge and as a result their

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

91

~rt of this effort was of great assistance to the Homes Endowment

soard.
The Inspectors' annual reports to the Grand Lecturer show that there
as
been an improvement in many of the Lodge problems. These reports
b indicate that there is still a long way to go before it can be said that
~Lodges of this Jurisdiction are all in a positive position. There is still a
t lack of community involvement by the me111bers of the Lodges in
~r respective School Boards, City Councils and other civic organiza-

. ns
bOD~e to the time schedule of our Annual Communication , I will cover
only two of the problems existing within the Lodges of this Jurisdiction.
One of the real vital problems is the advancement of Candidates through
the degrees. ln checking the records in the Grand Lodge Office, and as
111entioned by the Inspectors, regarding Candidates in a hold position as
either Entered Apprentices or Fellowcrafts, I was amazed at the number
of such Candidates. After talking to various officers and new members I
round that in many cases it was the lack of contact and concern on the part
of the officers, Candidate's coaches and members of the Lodge with these
Candidates. Brethren, these Candidates are your responsibility, and the
interest you show in their progress through the degrees of Masonry will be
reflected by a like interest in their own progress.
The following numbers are understated figures and are real eye-openers:
1. 371 of the Lodges have Candidates who have not advanced in over
one year from either Entered Apprentice to Fellowcraft or from Fellowcraft to Master Mason. One Lodge has 25 Candidates in this situation.
2. There are over 1188 Entered Apprentices who have not advanced in
over one year.
3. There are over 270 Fellowcrafts who have not advanced in over one
year.
In addition to pointing out a real problem that exists in many of our
Lodges, an ideal program presents itself for the incoming Masters and officers to pursue for 1982. Set a goal for yourselves of getting all these
Candidates back into the stream of Masonry. The following is just one of
many programs to undertake. Appoint a committee of active and Masonically educated members to make and keep a personal contact with each
Candidate. Give your personal guidance to this committee and also contact
each of the Candidates yourself. A successful program in this area could
well result in a turn-around in the loss of membership in many of the
Lodges.
As I mentioned previously, l am covering only two of the conditions that
currently exist in our Lodges. The second one is that of suspension for
non-payment of dues. There have been over 7000 members suspended for
non-payment of dues during the past 6 years. lt has been found that in
many cases these members are never personally contacted to ascertain the
reason for allowing their dues to lapse. It is the responsibility of each Lodge
to contact these members and, if necessary, to help them if it causes a
financial burden to pay their dues. lf this is not the case, convince the
member of your Lodge's interest in him and the need for his support and

interest in his own Lodge. Let this be true for all the members of your
Lodge; show an interest in them by personal contact. All the officers of
your Lodge should act as a committee for keeping in touch with your mem.
bers.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON DISTRIBUTION
To Tire Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
After reviewing the Grand Master's Annual Message, the Repo rts of the
Grand Treasurer, Grand Secretary, Masonic Ho mes Trustees , Masonic

f)istribut1 o n submtts the following repo rt:
GRAND MASTER'S MESSAGE

The Grand Maste r's Message contains three Recommendations and two
pecisions. We recommend that the subject ma tter invo lved in the Grand
Master's Message be referred to Committees as follows:
Recomme ndation No. 1 suggests that a Grand Lodge Committee be appainted to create and implement an effective program devised to reach the
r.tnk and tile of o ur membership. while directing its majo r emphasis to the
untapped source. the non-Mason. It was referred to the Committees on
Jurisprudence. Policy and General Purposes. Ritu al and Masonic Information and Responsibility.
Recommendation No. 2. recommending that advertising in Masonic
publicatio ns be permitted was referred to the Committees on Jurisprudence, Po licy and General Purposes and Commercialism .
Recommendati o n No. 3, wherein he recommends that policy be established by vote of this Grand Lodge which would permit any fu ture Grand
Master to arrange and sponsor a trip. Referred to the Committees on Jurisprudence. Policy and General Purposes and Commercialism.
Decision No. l. wherein the Grand Master stated th at a Lodge which
sponsor a DeMo lay Chapter has th e authority to expend its funds to pay
the registratio n fee for the advisors to the Chapter. Referred to Jurisprudence, Policy and General Purposes and Youth Committees .
Decision No. 2. wherein the Grand Master sta tes that public moneyraising schemes should not he indulged in by the prerequisite bodies. Referred to Jurisprudence and Commercialism Committees.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON
MASONIC SERVICE BUREAUS

MASONIC H OMES ENDOWMl-.NT BOARD

To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A . M. of California:
The Committee on Masonic Service Bureaus is pleased to present the
S4th Annual Report on its activities for the year ending June 30. 1981.
Th~ Right Worshipful Robert 0. West. Deputy Grand Master, was appointed liai on officer, and we appreciate his support and assistance during
the year.
The Officers and Representatives of the Service Bureaus practice charity
and benevolence and strive to promote human welfare. Throughout California , the Service Bureaus care for Sojourners. their widows and orphans,
operntc blood banks , arrange and conduct funerals for deceased Masons,
make investigations requested by Lodges of this or other jurisdictions, visit
sick Sojourners. support the programs of the Grand Master and practice
and promote fraternal relations with Sojourners.

We recommend that this report be referred in its entirety to the Committee on Finance.
Respectfully submitted .
VERNE

LF.R<>Y G . CONNELLY. Chairman

UNIFORM COMPACTS

A new Uniform Compact was approved for Saddleback Valley Lodge
No. 832 as a new member of the Orange County Masonic Service Bureau
Two Rivers Lodge No. 731, Tyre Lodge No. 741 and South Pasadena Lodg~
No. 362 are all new members of the Los Angeles Bureau following the
approval of a Uniform Compact.
MEETIN GS

The Comm ittee held four meetings durin g the year. One was h~ld during
Grand Lodge week. At that time many Officers and Representatives who
were also attending Grand Lodge. met with the Committee.
A group meeting was held on February 21. 1981 in Los Angeles. Our
guest speaker was Worshipful Ralph H. Hea<l . President of the Bush Masonic Relief and Editor of the California Freemason. This meeting was
attended by thirty-two Officers and Representatives of the Burea us located.
in Southern California.
A group meeting was held in Oakland on March 7 , 1981 fo r the Officers
and Representatives of the Bureaus located in Northern California. Our
guest speaker was Most Worshipful Edward H. Siems. Pase Grand Master
a nd past Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge. Twenty Officers and Representatives were present at this meeting.
A meeting was he ld in Los Angeles on June 10. 1981 to review the
budgets of the nineteen Bureaus and conduct other business that was presented to the Committee.
AUDITS

The Committee members review the financi al and administrative functions of th e Bureaus from time to time. This year the records of Glendale.
Orange Count y and San Bernardino Bureaus were reviewed. This is in
addition to the audit conducted by a Certified Public Accountant or an
experienced auditor that must be made each year.
The Service Bureaus are operating efficiently and according to the rules
and regulations established by the Committee. We compliment the Executive Secretary of all Bureaus for their work .
B UDGETS

Each of our Masonic Service Bureaus must present a budget for approval
on or before May lst each year. The Finance Committee of the Bureau is
responsible to study the financial affairs of the Bureau and make recommendations for the budget and per capita assessment for the ensuing year.
A per capita assessment by the Bureau to their member Lodges is based
on the total membership of the respective Lodges. not to exceed$ l .20 per

B USH MASONIC RELIEF

Worshipful Ralph H. H ead. President of t he Bush Masonic Relief. and
the Trustees provide the necessary funds for the operation of the six Masonic Service Bureaus located in the Greater Los Angeles Area.
The contributions amounted to 63% of the to tal b udgets for t he nineteen
Bureaus. The savings to the member Lodges is close to $3.50 per member
if a per capita assessment were necessary. The Masters a nd Wardens o f th e
member· Lodges join in expressing their appreciation to t he Trustees of the
Bush Masonic R elief.
TAXES

All Bureaus have filed information returns to the Internal Revenue Service on form 990 and to the Franchise Tax Board of the State of California
on either form 199 or 199 B. T he Los Angeles Bureau prepares forms other
than the 990 and 199. Bureaus requiring o ther tax repo rts have prepared
and filed the necessary forms on schedule.
ANNUAL REPORTS

All Bureaus have supplied the Annual Reports to the Committee. They
include the Election Report, Budget Report. Statistical and Financial Reports, Operating Expenses and Blood Bank Activities .
The Service Bureaus conducted over 600 Maso nic funera l services for
Sojourne rs. Over 500 visits to sick Sojourners were made by the Representatives o f the Bureaus. Nearly 350 investigatio ns were made at the request of other jurisdictions or at the request of th e Grand Secretary. The
Executive Secretary of th e Burea us assisted in preparing about 80 applications to Masonic Ho mes . both in our jurisdiction and in other jurisdictions.
It is through the un tiring efforts of the Executive Secretaries. t he Officers and Represt!ntatives t hat we have a strong. viable network of Bureaus
in this Jurisdiction - the backbone of an important and worthwhile program to assist our Sojourners.
We anticipate an increasing need to assist Sojourners and their families.
t?gether with a continued need, in the years to come. to provide professional assistance that is available through our Executive Secretaries.
BLOOD BANKS

~en of the Bureaus operate a blood hank for their member Lodges and
Sojourners. During the year. th ere were about 1.800 pints of blood do-

CALIFORNIA MASONIC MEMORIAL TEMPLE

the auditorium; retiling of committee rooms and the exhibition hall; and
recovering of the auditorium benches.
The completion of the elevator repairs to meet OSHA earthquake requirements continued to be a significant cost factor. We are pleased to
announce that this OSHA elevator project has been accomplished in a
timely manner and in conformity to law. Our final major project was the
renovation of the ceiling over the garage entrance.
Two other elements combined to provide us with a negative financial
picture for the year. By the very nature of several of the necessary repair
projects, we were unable to fully rent our auditorium during a four-month
period. This affected our income position significantly. In compliance with
a revision and restructuring of our financial statement by Grand Lodge, we
suffered a one-time loss from the adjustment of stocks to current value as
well as a modification of items expensed versus those capitalized.
A thorough examination by the Board leads us to no other conclusion
but that the Temple is being efficiently managed, the present policies are
sound, and our financial stance should reflect considerable improvement
next year.
Brother Loren Stritenberger continues to demonstrate loyal, consciencious, and sound management in his position as Executive Vice President
and General Manager of the Temple. We are most fortunate to have him
serve us in these two positions.
Upon the appointment by our Grand Master of Robert A. Klinger as
Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge, Brother Klinger assumed the duties
as Secretary of our Board of Trustees. He immediately immersed himself
into his duties on the Board, and we are extremely grateful for the outstanding services he has provided us.

To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Board of Trustees of the California Masonic Memorial Temple hereby
submits its 26th Annual Report.
At the close of the 1980 Annual Communication of Grand Lodge, the
Board of Trustees of the California Masonic Memorial Temple held its
meeting. The Board of Trustees then proceeded to nominate and elect the
following officers to serve for the ensuing year:

Harold S. Stein, Jr.
Mark E. Schrock
John A. Sickenberger
Verne W. Hendrix

President
Vice President
Treasurer
Secretary

The California Masonic Memorial Temple serves as a patriotic monument and memorial, open to the public, commemorating the members of
the armed services of the United States and of the Most Worshipful Grand
Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the States of California and Hawaii
who gave their lives in battle during World War II. With this definition in
mind, it is incumbent upon the Trustees to maintain the facility and to
permit it to function within the spirit associated with an historic monument
of great Masonic significance. The Trustees can report with confidence that
all those persons associated with the operation and maintenance of the
California Masonic Memorial Temple have faithfully discharged their duties.
During the course of the year, the Trustees have embarked upon a program of inventorying and re-evaluating all policies relative to the Masonic
Memorial Temple and its properties.
The Trustees and Temple staff have made several physical inspections of
the pre!'1ises and the garage facilities. The Board has taken positive steps
to momtor the appearances of the garage, that it may continue to function
practically yet in conformity with our standards.
It has examined all aspects of the operation and administration of our
Pine Street properties.
Two special assignments have been initiated during the year, to be completed during the course of the upcoming year. A sub-committee has been
formed to review and present all actions of previous Temple Boards that
represent stated policy. These will be reviewed, condensed, and if necessary modified, and presented in a final document for reference and to orient any new, future members to the Board.
Another sub-committee is investigating the performance record and current and projected status of the garage facility in anticipation of the 1983
lease anniversary.
It was necessary this year to schedule a significant amount of monies for
needed repairs and refurbishing of our facilities. Some of the major work
accomplished included recarpeting of both the main floor and balconies of

It has held the conventions for:

REPORT OF THE INVESTMENT COMMITTEE
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Investment Committee reports on the condition of the invested funds
of all Grand Lodge entities, including the Endowment and General Funds
of the Masonic Homes of California for the fiscal year ended, June 30,
1981. The Committee is cognizant of its responsibility in causing the funds
to produce the highest return commensurate with the continuing preser'mtion of capital.
The Investment Committee meets quarterly with its investment counselors and with representatives of the financial institution chosen to evaluate the performance of its investment policies and practices.
At the end of the fiscal year, the total market value of the Endowment
Fund was $37,640,000 with an annualized yield of 8.99%. Annual income
is estimated at $3,397 ,000 with fixed income securities representing 65%
of the total portfolio value and convertible bonds and common stocks 35 % .
The market value of the General Fund investments of the Masonic Homes
was $26,013,000. The yield of 10.5% is estimated to produce an annual
income of $2,732,000. The Fund has 67% in fixed income securities, which
like the Endowment Fund, consist of United States Government and Fed~
eral Agency obligations, corporate and other financial organization bonds,
and money market securities. The remainder of the Fund, or 33% was in
common stocks.
In addition to the Masonic Home funds, the Investment Committee su~rvises a portfolio of funds of Grand Lodge, California Masonic Memonal Temple, and eighteen restricted use funds for the benefit of the Masonic Homes. The investment of funds of the California· Masonic Foundation

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

and Amaranth Funds and the Pooled Income Fund are also under its direction. These various funds totaled $2,988,000 in market value with a
yield of 11.8% and an estimated annual income of $462,000.
The market value of the total portfolio on June 30, 1981, was $67,585,000
compared to $64,547 ,000 a year ago. Annualized yield for the 1980-81 fiscal
year was 9.8%.
The Pooled Income Fund should be of especial interest to the members
of Grand Lodge. At year's end the market value of the Fund was $944,000
with a yield of I0.15% based on original investment. Masons and friends
of the Fraternity may contribute assets for the eventual benefit of the Masonic Homes. In the meanwhile, the donors receive a lifetime income and
may realize certain tax advantages.
It should be recognized that the funds of the Masonic Homes and those
of Grand Lodge have been accumulated and continue to grow only because
of the generous support of the Masons of California, both living and dead.
This beneficence has made possible the operations of the Masonic Homes
and the educational and charitable grants of Grand Lodge.
The rate of inflation, rising interest rates, Federal deficit spending and
other factors have combined to bring intense presstue on the investment
market. While fixed income securities are reported at market value, the
maturity value of these securities is appreciably higher. The general high
quality of these bOnds-Government, Federal Agencies, and corporate with
ratings between AA and AAA and with average maturities of six yearshelps to assure that the underlying value of the portfolio is greater than
the reported market value.
In the atmosphere of the times the funds of Grand Lodge and its entities
have been invested in a largely defensive manner, intent on preserving
capital. At the same time every effort is made to produce the highest revenue and capital gains possible.
Despite the vagaries of the marketplace, the Investment Committee continues to believe in and have faith in the economic future of the United
States.

During the fiscal year July 1, 1980 to June 30, 1981, we awarded 64
1eholarships from the General Fund; 29 from the Amaranth Fund and 3
from the Mendenhall Fund. The total thereof is in the sum of $70,440.00.
Grants in the sum of $2,000.00 each were made, for educational and
~adership training programs, to the Northern and Southern Jurisdictions,
Order of DeMolay; Grand Guardian Council of California, International
Order of Job's Daughters; International Order of Rainbow in California.
Grants in the sum of $2,000.00 each were made to the Crippled Children's Societies of Los Angeles and Santa Clara Counties.
It is the consensus of your Board of Trustees that available funds should
be devoted to scholarship awards and that no other grants be made except
those for educational and leadership training programs to Youth Orders.
Unless we are instructed otherwise by this Grand Lodge, or by the Most
Worshipful Grand Master, we will, in the future, act in accordance with
that consensus.
The investments, income and expense of the Foundation are set forth in
the Report of the. Grand Treasurer, and therefore, are not repeated here.
We have succeeded in holding our direct Trustee expense to approximately
9.4% of income, despite the greatly increased cost of transportation, printing, etc., caused principally by changes in the personnel of the Board,
requiring the establishment of new and different administrative procedures. Some of this expense is non-recurring.
All outstanding loans and loan balances, originally made from the Altenberg Fund have been collected in full and said Fund has been transferred to our General Fund.
Contributions and donations in the sum of $8,624.00 were received during the fiscal year, for which our appreciation has been appropriately expressed. We also hereby express our special appreciation of the continued
efforts of Brothers John Hunt, Everett Houser and Chester R. MacPhee,
P.G.M. on behalf of the Foundation.
We expect to receive an increasing number of applications for scholarship awards due to the increased cost of education. We therefore solicit
increased participation of all Masons in California and Hawaii in the enCouragement of donations and contributions to our Foundation.

The Committee was called upon to advise t h e usua l number of Masons

the opinion of the Committee was requested on a number of activit ies by

as follows:

1. Rental of Lodge refreshment hall for rummage sales, bazaar sales,
book sales, garden sales anJ blood hanks hy a variety of organizatio ns.

These and many other issues we re dealt with. using good counsel. and
no Maso ni c trials resulted .
On N ove mber 7. 1980. the Committee received a request from a Temple
Association. along with other Masonic affiliatcJ groups. as to t he legality
of a fireworks booth operated by such group~. Section 2070 C.M.C. states.
"A Lodge shall not sponsor. or by resolution or otherwise sa nction. or
permit the use of. the name of the Lodge in connection with. or for the
purpose of furthering any collateral financial unde rtaking. or commercial
venture. whether for profit or not. which shall 1101 have been approved by
the Grand /'.Jaster."
Our o pinio n. simply stated. was that it is within the scope of the law. if
approved by the Grand Master. We made no comment a~ to the propriety
of the venture . leaving thar as a discretionary Jecision by the Grand Ma~­
ter.
In May of this year a copy of the Knights Templar Magazine. a national
publicat ion distributed in California. was given to the Committee with at·
tentio n called to several advertisements contained therein. This was immediate ly mailed to the Grand Master, with the note that the violations
were self-evident. and with the suggestion that it required attention from
the highest Masonic level. As of the writing of this repo rt we have no
information regarJing its disposition.
It has been the custom of the Committee to review the financia~ reports
of the several Shrine Charity Events (2070d C.M.C.). however. only the
Baker fie kl and H o nol ulu reports were submitteJ to the Committee . These
were found to be in o rtler. We make no report on t he o thers.
The Committee on Com mercialism tloes not initiate investigations. It is
not the duty of the Committee to "patrol" the Craft in search of violations,
but ra ther, its activities originate with requests. or complaints which are
referred to the Committee.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON
CONSTITUTION OBSERVANCE
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge. F & A. M. of Cal~fomia:
The writers of the U. S. Constitution described that immortal document
as "the new order of the ages··. It is engraved on our dollar bills. To paraphrase, the Committee understands it to continue to be the '"new order of
the World". It may be time again to engrave upon our minds the words of
the "Father of our Country", one of our greatest Americans. our First
President and our Brother. George Washington: "Citizens by birth or choice,
of a common country. that country has a right to concentrate your affections. The name of AMERICAN. which belongs to you ... must always
exalt the just pride of patriotism, more than any appellation derived from
local discriminations. With slight shades of diffe rence . vou have the same
religion . manners , habits and -political principles. You have in a common
cause fought and triumphed together. The independence and liberty yo u
possess arc the work of joint councils. and joint efforts; of commo n dangers. sufferings and successes."
(OMMITTEF PURPOSE

"TO INSPIRE EVERY YOUNG GENERATION AND THEIR ELDERS , ANNUALLY. TO A BETTER UNDERSTANDING AND
PRACTICE OF T HE LAWS OF THE CONSTITUTION OF THE
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA."
MASO!'<I C U. S. CoNST ITL' TION OBSERVANCE

The Committee continues to serve as it has done for forty-five ( 45) years.

Jiving. exert a powerful attractive force which continues to draw good men
to our Fraternity. Tu the extent to which we practice it, we as individuals
are uplifted and enabled. To the extent to which we practice it , our communities are better places in which to live. To the extent to which we practice pure Freemasonry. men arc attracted to our Fraternity. and we prosper
and grow. To the extent to which we practice pure Freemasonry. our Lodge
rooms will be full to overflowing.
There is a second kind of Freemasonry which we might call organizational Freemasonry. It involves all of the things which we do in trying to
accomplish our ideals-the way in which we organize our Lodges and our
Grand Lodge, the activities of our Concordant and Appendent Bodies. the
maintenance of our Temples. our committees. our ofticers. For many of us
organizational Freemasonry occupies most of our time and on it we expend
much of our e nergy. This Grand Lodge Communication is a feast for those
of us who love to make the wheels of our Masonic machine go round. How
caught up we sometimes are in the intracacies! And sometimes we, even
you and I, must be reminded that the object of all these activities is the
furtherance of the ideals of the true Freemasonry.
All of us here in this auditorium this afternoon though dedicated to the
first kind of Freemasonry are deepl y involved in the second kin<l .
Is it possible that on occasion we become so deeply enmeshed in the
organizational details of our Brotherhood that we lose sight of our ideals'?
Are there times when our very organizational structure gets in the way of
the accomplishment of our goals? I believe that there is evidence that this
may be the case. I believe that many of the prohlems over which we agonize at such length and into whose solution we put so much effort can be
analyzed in these. terms. Let's get down to cases.
We have all been concerned with the large numher of candidates who
fail to advance beyond the first degree. Ahout one candidate in five pays
our fees, knocks at our door. becomes an E ntered Apprentice and is not
seen again within the precincts of our Lodge halls. If this were an occasional circumstance we might be justified in thinking that the man had
made a mistake in applying and di<l not desire to continue: but experience
tells us that in most cases the man who has just been initiated is more
e~thused about Masonry than he will ever be again. Why then <lo we lose
him? Could it be because we don 't include him in the activities of the
Lodge because he's only an Entered Apprentice? Could it be that he loses
intere t because for several months his only link with the Lodge is his
coach? We must rea lize that the man who comes to us isn 't interested in
just the d egrees of which he knows little. but that he has a whole range of
social needs which he hopes the Lodge will help to meet. He has the need
for fellowship with other men of high ideals . He has the need to be involved in some socially useful activitv. He ha!) the need to he entertained
in an uplifting way. A~d yes. he has the need to be recognized as a familv
man whose wife and even children should he drawn within the circle de
fellowship. Perhaps he <loesn's return because we've offered him Brotherly
Love, Relie f and Truth. but he perceives that our organization is not interested in him as a person. but only as a "Candidate". We de lay too long

SPAIN
The "Grand Oriente Espanol" was furni shed a copy of a letter mailed
by the Master of Arthur T. Weed Lodge No. 59 (a Military Lodge under
the Jurisdiction of the National Grand Lodge of France) located in Madrid
which carried an endorsement upon it bearing the Seal of "Grand Oriente
Espanol " purporting to give "regularity" to themse lves. and was then circulated throughout the "Masonic World."' This resulted in some confusion,
but worse "contempt and detestation·· and the most severe disciplinary
action against the now former Brother who furnished the letter. A recent
communication from the National Grand Lodge of France reveals that in
addition to the four (4) Military Lodges unde r their jurisdiction in Spain,
they have consecrated a District Grand Lodge of Spain composed of six
(6) Lodges which admit Spanish citizens to membership . A list of the above
Lodges and their locations are attached to this report.
ITALY
The news media and enemies of Freemasonry have had a " he yday" in
Italy, but their efforts were spent upon a clandestine organization which
was also deceiving Freemasonry. This, then. gives Universal Freemasonry
no reason to depart from its time honored customs. principles. and practices of supporting regular Masons. Lodges and Grand Lodges wherever
they may be located .
The subject Lodge. Propaganda-No. 2, or simply ··r-2" was founded in
1887 for the purpose of admitting to membership chose men who were
otherwise qualified to receive the degrees of Masonry, but did not possess
the requirement of residence within the jurisdiction of the loca l Lodges in
Rome. It was provided that the Grand Master would always be the Master
of this "Special Lodge". and it served Masonry well until destroyed by
Fascism in 1925. Following World War IL in 1960. the G rand Master appointed Licio Ge Iii to reorganize and reactivate the P-2 Lodge. This Lodge
then appeared to prosper and do well, but in the early seventies irregularities began to surface indicating clandestine activities, and in l 97.t the Grand
Lodge in regular Communication ordered P-2 dissolved and dismantled.
This o rde r was not properly carried out. and in 1976 Lodge P-2 and its
Master Licio Gelli were expelled and the Lodge Charter cancelled.
Subsequent to the above action by the Grand Lodge in 1976 the "Gelli
Group" as it became known . continued their clandestine activity and it was
learned that the G rand Master. Lino Salvini, was giving "aid and comfort"
to the "Ge lli Group" so he. too. was expelled. Ennio Battclli was then
elected Grand Maste r but is powerless to control the irregular clandestine
"Gelli G ro up ." Brother Battelli has convened meetings of the Executive
Committee of the Grand Lodge and offered to resign, but the Committee
decided that he should continue in office at least until the Special Com-

REPORT OF THE SPECIAL COMMITTEE
ON INSURANCE STUDY
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M . of Ca lifornia:
At the 13lst Annual Communication, a resolution was adopted by 5/6
affirmative vote directing the incoming Grand Master to see to the implementatio n of Recommendations I and 2 in the report of the undersigned ,
dated October 14, 1980. On October 30, 1980, the Grand Master reappointed the undersigned for that purpose. and we report as follows :

I. R ECOMMENDATION 1.

As discussed in our 1980 Report. Mr. Clarence R. Atwood. of Atwood
& Co., Consulting Actuaries, has determined that a self-insurance program

for all entities which presently secure their insurance through the Grand
Lodge as well as those Masonic Temple Associations which wish to participate in this program would provide substantial savings for all participants
and would therefore be economically feasible. Our 1980 Report suggested
two vehicles to implement a self-insurance program : an insurance trust and
an inter-insurance exchange. Because the total annual premium for all insurance carried by the Masonic Temple Associations in this jurisdiction as
well as all policies administered through the G rand Lodge is too low at this
time to make an inter-insurance exchange economically fe asible, our 1980

The Committee on Insurance:
Our Insurance Committee has reviewed the report of the Special Committee, and we are in agreement with th e intent and purpose of the ir deliberations to a rrive at some method where by the cost of insurance for our
Masonic Temple Associatio ns and other Masonic insurance might he reduced.
It has been the purpose of our Committee to he alert to any possible
premium saving for o ur Temple Associations as dem o nstrated in our annual report to G rand Lodge in 1979 in which we advised the Temples of a
possible saving of thirty percent for fire and liab ility insurance and a lso
again in ou r report of July .1. 1981 sent to the Temples in o ur report "Recommendation for Compre hensive Cove rage for Temple Associations."
The report of th e Special Committee reco mmends that the forma tio n of
an Insurance Trust. previously proposed in their report of October 14, 1980
should not be fo rmed at this time.
Our Committee is in agreement with this recommendation due to the
complications involved .
The Special Committee also suggests that a committee of Grand Lodge
should pe riod ically conside r the advisability of establishing an Insurance
Trust or an inte r-insurance exchange when economically advisable.
In view o f the fact th at our Co mmittee has researched this propositio n
over the past three years , the responsibility for th e continuing study of the
questions sho uld rem a in with our regular Insurance Committee instead of
a special committee.
The report of the Special Committee questions whether o ur Masonic
in surance has been adequately mar keted and suggests co mpetitive bidding
to secure lower premiums.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON TEMPLE PROPERTIES
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Your Committee on Temple Properties is pleased to submit its Annual
Repo rt for the 1980-81 Grand Lodge year. Again we have had another
year of high interest rates making it even more difficult to finance new
buildings. T he pressures of inflation are continuing to place greater burdens on the operations of our Temples and the search for additional income
to carry the extra cost increases. If the Associations must raise the rents.
the Lodges may be forced to increase their dues.
According to a portion of the Form 2oo·s received d uring the period, a
considerable amount of the reports do not reflect any depreciation allowances. All you aFe doing by omitting this cost control is to kid yourselves.
When the funds become necessary. they will not be available.
The requirements of CMC 1208 are being ignored by some of the Associations either through lack of knowledge or deliberate omission. Without obtaining permission, the members of the Associations could become
personall y liable in case of problems . Actually. seeking our permission and
obtaining it cou ld help to get you off the hook and put it on us.
We are still having trouble with the item of REPAIRS. No definitive
answer has been made as to whether or not REPAIRS come under our
jurisdiction . Sect. 1208 of CMC says "CONSTRUCTION. ALTERATION
OR IMPROVEMENT of a Masonic Temple". We would like to know about
repairs. but it is not specifically covered.
Your Committee is still trying to compile a complete listing of all the
real estate properties owned directly. or indirectly. by the member Lodges
of this Jurisdiction. We are getting closer. A t least we kn ow who has not
sent the information required . Together wit h the Grand Secretary's office.
we are closing in on yo u non-filers.
We have had considerable activity this Masonic year. Even requests to
erect new Temples. Ho wever, the tinancing of these have been tricky and
very long in arranging.

mquiries have been directed to members of the Committee and we have

Concern was expressed this past year that we as Masons and also as
individuals. do no t and cannot condone some of the things that a re being
done in our local ~choo ls. and th at we must be careful no t to le t the general
puhlic be of the opinion that we app rove all the actions and programs of
our local school districts. Wh at we do encourage and promote is the concept of free public education.
Dee p concern is still felt by the Public Schoob Committee of Grand
Lodge that too many Lodges. particularly in the metropolitan areas, consider that they have accomplished their Masonic duty and respo nsibility by
participating in a large joint effort with other Lodges and/or Districts in a
Public Schools Weck Observance. T he Committee congratulates these
Lodges in their joint efforts and certainly encourages their continuance .
However. each Lodge should be awa re that the re arc numerous April and
year round projects for individual Lodge participation. The Committee
encourages each Lodge to have a "project of their own'". Many ideas and
suggestions are contained in the green pages of the Lodge Manual. Your
Grand Lodge Committee on Public Schools is ready and willing to be of
any assistance desired by the Lodges and Maste rs .

To The Mosr Worshipful Grand Lodge. F & A. M. of California:

The members of the Laymen's Night Speakers Panel arc pleased to submit the following report of activities for the 1980-1981 Grand Lodge year.
Since the creation of the Laymen's Night Speakers Panel in 1978. members of this Committee hJve traveled this Jurisdiction from north to south,
and from Island to Island spreading the light of Masonry to non-Mason
Jnd Mason alike . Lodges desiring to hold a Laymen's Night program have
only to schedule an evening 2-3 months in advance and contact t.he Chairman of this Committee directlv. or through the Grand Lodge office. and a
knowledgeable speaker will b~ furnished without cost to the sponsoring
Lodge.
During the 1980- 1981 Grand Lodge year .58 Lo~ges in the southern IJ<?f·
tion of the Jurisdiction availed themselves of this opportunrty. L1kew1se
approximately 2.5 Lodges in the northern portion of the state participated
in the program. In total 83 Lodges throughout the Jurisdiction , or 14%,
.
participated.
Some Lodges arc now planning their fifth annual Laymen's Night program. Make no mistake. membership solicitation is not our goal: ho.wever,
many good men never seek out our privileges because they know ltttle or
nothing about Masonry. or because they are waiting to he invited to r.articipate in our privileges. This program provides a vehicle for ac4uamttng
such a non-Mason with our Fraternity anc.l at the ~am c time provides a
stimulus toward more active participation by our present members.

To Tire Mose Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Immediately aft~r last year's Annual Communication your Lodge Re·
sources Development Committee was assigned by the Grand Master the
task of establishing a new program . This program was to stimulate support
of and increase participation in Lodge activities hy its members. The Masonic Light Award was the result of this effort and was introduced into our
Grand Jurisdiction early this past year. rt is anticipated that the results of
the program will be published in the Spring issue of the California Freemalon Magazine.
Your Committee has also been actively supporting Lodges which arc
having trouble obtaining officers, new members . etc. Inevitably this has
led to a discussion of Lodge consolidation or merger. As most of you arc
aware Lodge consolidations are enjoying increased popularity and are on
the upswing in our Grand Jurisdiction. During the past decade of the seventies alone, more Lodge consolidations have occurred than throughout
the previous one hundred and thirty years of our Grand Lodge's existence.
It's been said that "consolidation is only a sign of the times", that "all
organizations are declining in membership and attendance."
But , my Brethren , Lodge consolidations are a COP OUT! They're not
necessary nor do they solve the problem that caused the Lodge to seek
consolidation in the first place. To the contrary. many organizations are
growing and so are many of our Lodges. What are they doing that the rest

of us are not? A lmost without exception those Lodges that are successrut

grams more than a year in advance and avoid the last minute scramblina
to " put something together ... And they plan regularly scheduled programs
for their familie s and neighbo rs. involving the community in their pro.
grams.
No, my Brethren . it doesn't have to he "a sign of the times". You don't
have to consolidate with another Lodge. You can turn your Lodge around
and see it grow. But it won 't be easy am.I it won't come for free. We know
that you've tried all these things before. But. we believe that with a sys.
tematic approc.u.:h using these programs the result will he a positive growth
in your Lodge. It can be done ! It has hccn <lone !
Don't wait until it's too late and the only choice you ha,·e is como lidation
or Joss of eharter. Take positive steps now! If you need help or some sug.
gestions. then call on your Lodge Resources Development Committeewe·re here to help you.

REPORT OF THE COMMIT TEE ON TAXATION
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M . of California:
The Committee on Taxation serves to render advice when requested by
~e _G~and Lodge. subordinate Lodges. and organization s under their jurisd1ct1on with respect to matters of taxation. This advice includes the
Committee ·s annual report which discusses items of current interest in the
taxation of fraternal organiza tions.

PROCEEDI NGS O F THE

G R A~ D LO DGE OF CALIFORN IA

We have been asked whether the re arc any tax consequences to Lodges
who charge for dinners or other programs. particularly if the charge is in
excess of the actual cost of the eve nt . thereby returning a profit to the
Lodge. Lodges are taxa ble on income from a trade or business which is
unrelated to the fratern al purposes of the Lodge. Lodge fund raising events
do not typically constitute a trade or bu siness. To constitute a trade or
business, the activity must be regularly carried on . This does not include
periodic fund raising eve nts. Operating a restaurant constitutes a trade or
business. Holding periodic fund raisi ng d inners docs no t constitute a trade
o r business. In addition . income fro m fund raising events conducted by tax
exempt fraternal org::tnizations, such as Masonic Lodges, are not tuxable if
substantially all the la bo r required to ho ld the event is performed for the
Lodge witho ut compensation.
In addition to income tax consequences. there are potential sales tax
consequences to Lodge fu nd raising events. A 6lk sales tax is assessed
upon the s<i lc of tangi ble personal propert y. The sale of tangible personal
property indudes furni shing meals as well as supplying merchandise at
garage sales or bazaars. for a purchase price. e ven if the purchase price is
labeled a "donation ... There is one exemption to the tax available to Lodges,
however. Social clubs and fratern al o rganizations. such as Masonic Lodges,
arc not subject to the sales tax o n their receipts from furnishing meals if
the meals arc furni shed exclusively to members and are furn ished less freque ntl y than once a week . Both these requirements must be met. If the
Lodge furnishes meals to non-mcmhers. all rece ipts from meals are subject
to tax, whether the meals are furnished to members or non-members.
However. meals paid for by members are considered furnished to the members and are therefore not subject to the sales tax e\'en though consumed
by guests who are not members. The Committee suggests that ti ckets for
non-me mbers who <i ttend Lodge fun d raising dinne rs should he purchased
by members of the Lodge. The Lodge need not thewafter conce rn itself
with whethe r the member o btains any reimhursement from the guest. Any
other transfers of tangible personal property by the Lodge at fund raising
events. such as garage sales or bazaars, are subject to th e 6<fc sales tax. If
the Lodge is subj ect to the sa les tax. it must apply for a California Seller's
permit. These are obtained from the local oftice of the State Board of
·
.
Equalization .
The Committee has also been asked whether o r no t Lodges arc required
to pay sales tax when they purchase fro m printers their comple ted Trestle
Board or othe r Lodge bulletin for distribution to members. As di<;cussed
above . with respect to Lodge dinn er~ and other fund raising events. the
sale of tangible personal propert y is subject to the sales tax. A printer's
charge fo r printing your bulletin is considered the sale of tangible personal
propert y: the bulletin . However. the law provides an exemptio n for the
sale of .. periodicals'·. A periodica l is a publication issued at stated intervals.
which publication contains news o r in formation of ge neral inte rest to a
particul ar organizatio n. A Lodge bull::!tin which is no more than a notice
of upcoming meetings does not qualify as a pe riodical containing " news or
informatio n of general interest ... However. a LoJ ge bulletin which contains

rtides and other info rmation in additio n to upcoming events has been
~led exempt from the sales tax. If your Lodge hulletin does contain news
nd informatio n other than upcoming dates. and you arc paying sales tax
: your printer for printing the bulletin. you should advise the printer that

you are exempt as a period ic.ii. [f the printe r is unwilling to recognize this
exemption . th e State Board of Equalizution or your Committee should be
contacted .

The Committee 011 Ritual:
The proponent s of this resolution arc to be commende d for their study
of the organizati on and structure of the Grand Lodge. However, they are
taking. an idealistic point of view and using ideal circumstances to estahtish
their criteria, when they limit. by legislation . the tenure of Inspectors to
nine years.
.
The informal understand ing that Inspector~ serve at least tive, hut not
more than ten years, has worked very well because of flexibility. Th_~ PoS·
itivc limitation that ··No Inspector shall serve more than nine ye.ars does
not allow for any c-ircumstance that may arise. where an ex~ept1on might
be essential. This absolute restriction might he very undesirabl e on and
after 1990; and the years to follow. when this resolution becomes totally
effective.
This Jurisdiction contains many small Lodges. some in very remote areas.
Small membersh ips in Jnspectoral Districts do not lend themselves . t? a
great number of qualified people Qualified people •.ire. not always wllhng
or able to serve and unfortunat ely the numbers are limited .
We agree that a limit on tenure has thcoreticctl merit. but do not believe
it is practical in all cases . It is not necessary to usc leg1sla~1on in. hcu of
good judgment. Tenure o f office for Inspectors should remain fkx1ble .
Your Committe e on Ritual recommen ds a " No"' vote.

The Committee 011 Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. l.t seeks to change the name of Hollywood-Melrose Lodge
No. 355. F. & A. M .. to its former name of Hollywood Louge No. 355, F.
&A.M .
This Louge has endeavored to follow the California Masonic Code sec·
tions which were considered to apply to this situation. Howner. the Code
is silent as to specific procedure to be followed in rega rd to the change of
a Lodge name. either before or after a consolidation. except for the state·
ment in Section 2022. which states that the Lodge name and number may
be changed only by Grand Lodge.

(iKAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

245

Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes therefore believes that

ill the future, additions to the Code should be made so as to clarify the

procedura l steps to be taken hy a Lodge in order to change its name.
Hollywood-Melrose Lodge in good faith has followed what appears to
be all of the available procedure~ for seeking a change of name. However.
we believe that no policy is involved in the selection of the name and.
therefore , make no recommendation.
In order to place the resolution before the Grand Lodge. I move its
adoption . without recommendation .

_WHEREAS: from its inception in 1850 until 1953. a period of 103 years.
thts Grand Junsd1ct1on and its concordant Masonic bodies prospered and

Master Masons be proficient in the Candidate's Lecture of the Master Mason Degree before applying for, or receiving any degree, or being initiated

in any Lodge, Order or Organization. the prerequisite of membership
wherein is that a person be a Master Mason; and
WHEREAS. during the past 28 years, the requirement of the proficien
in the Candidate's Lecture of the Master Mason Degree has created ~
unequal double standard of pre-1953 and post-1953 Master Masons; and
WHEREAS. a Master Mason may, without the requirement of a profi.
ciency in the Candidate's Lecture of the Master Mason Degree. participate
.in all his Blue Lodge activities. attend Stated Meetings. cast his ballot upon
new candidates, participate in the conferral of degrees, visit other Lodges
and may even serve as an Appointive Officer of his Lodge; and
WHEREAS, Master Masons who received their degrees in another rec.
ognizcd Grand Lodge Jurisdiction that does not require the proficiency in
the Candidate 's Lecture of the Master Mason Degree. can establish residence in our Jurisdiction and make application to an affiliated Masonic
organization without the requirement of the proficiency; and
WHEREAS, this proficiency requirement has placed an unjust and unequitable restriction upon a vast number of Master Masons who, due to
age, personal or extenuating circumstances have not obtained the profi.
ciency and are therefore deprived of seeking further light in Masonry which
can be beneficial to Blue Lodges; and
WHEREAS, it is strongly believed that the amended waiting period as
proposed allows sufficient time and opportunity for a new Master Mason
to become an active member of his Lodge.

or Organization the prerequisite of membership wherein is that a person

Your Committee on Jurisprudence to which Resolution No. 37 has been
referred. reports as follows:
The proponents of this resolution seek to provide that Master Masons
may seek membership in concordant bodies upon satisfying either of the
following:

l. By giving satisfactory evidence by strict examination in open Lodge
that he is proficient and qualified in the Candidate's Lecture of the
Degree of Master Mason and until after the lapse of one year from
the date he received the Degree of Master Mason; or
2.

In the absence of such proficiency examination that a period of two
years has passed from the date he received the Degree of Master
Mason.

To carry out the intent of the proponents, your Committee submits the
following legislation:
RESOLVED. that Section 2635 of the California Masonic Code be
amended to read as follows:
"Sec. 2635. MEMBERSHIP IN PREREQUISITE ORGANIZATIONS. A Mason who applied and was elected subsequent to October
1953 to receive the degrees of Masonry in a Lodge of this Jurisdiction
shall not apply for nor receive any degree or be initiated into any organization . other than another Lodge, the prequisite of membership wherein
is that a person be a Mason , until either he has given satisfactory evidence, by strict examination in open Lodge. that he is proficient and
qualified in the Candidate's Lecture of the Degree of Master Mason and
until after the lapse of one year from the date he receives the Degree of
Master Mason or in the absence of the aforesaid proficiency and qualification that there be a lapse of two years from the date that he received
the Degree of Master Mason. This section docs not apply to organizations which do not confer degrees and do not have formal initiation
ceremonies ."

the Resolution.

Good accou nting practice (and present Masonic law) re4uires a separii.
tion of accounting procedures so that the independent reports of two or
more persons may confirm the accuracy of each other's reports. This now
occurs when the Lodge Treasurer and Secretary independently report as
required by Sections 2546 and 25-t8 of the California Masonic Code.
Section 254X. 4th. California Masonic Code requires the Secretay "to
collect and receive all moneys due to the Lodge and pay them over to the
Treasurer." It docs not make sense for the Secretary to be charged with
collecting moneys due the Lodge and then for the Treasurer to be permitted to make a report on Lodge income.
The Grand Lodge of California now requires reports at December 31
and June 30 because these dates coincide with the Grand Lodge fiscal year.
To permit reports from Constituent Lodges at various dates depending
upon the Lodge fiscal year would create une4ual reporting to and fro m the
Grand Lodge or cause considerahle extra work on th e part of the Grand
Lodge staff to convert a Lodge ·s fiscal year reports to a calendar year basis.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON FINANCE
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge. F & A . M. of California:
In accordance with the requirements of o ur Code. the Grand Treasure r
has presented aud ited financi al statements for the fiscal year ended June
30, 1981. Those reports reveal that the costs to operate your Grand Lodge
during the past tiscal year rose nearl y twelve percent (12% ), a reasonable
increa e in the present economic climate .
Although your Committee on Finance is principally interested in . a nd
charged with the responsibility of establishing a budget for the operatio nal
expen e of the Grand Lodge. we are also very concerned with the control
of tho e expe nses. and. in ass isti ng all in volved with expenditures, to observe the budgetary limitations.
Supplementary appro priations for those items where budgets were exlleeded. totaled $63.500 .00 and were duly a pproved by the Grand Master.
Of special interest are two items which accounted for mo re than half of
that amount : "Grand Lodge Ofticers' Travel '' of $70 .000, exceeded the
budget by $20,400. and the "Public Schools Committee" net expense of
132.000, exceeded their budget by $18.(XlO. We express o u r appreciation to
all Committ ee C hairmen for th e prudent management of their budgets.

NOTE l • SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES:
The fi nancia l statements of Masonic H0tnes of Galif ornia have beeu

policies follOW' :
Fund Accounting:

Othe r Asset s :
Other assets consist of life i nsurance polic ies, real estate and
mineral rights assigned or bequeathed t o the Masonic Homes.
Real estate and mineral rights are recorded at the nominal value
of $1 each for acc oun tability. Pa}'lllents by the Masonic Romes of obligations of the assignors secured by these assets are added to the nominal

To insure obse rvance of limitations and restrictions placed on the
use of resources available to the Homes, the accounts of the Homes are
maintained in accorda nce with the princ iple s of fund accounting .

value,

The as se ts, liabilities and fund balances of the Homes are reported
in three self-balancing funds, as follow:

Life ins urance policies are r ecorded at their a ctuar ily detennined
present values .

General Fund - Resources are available t o support the

Permanent Endowment Fund - Ordinances of the Grand Lodge
provide that no portion of the principal of the Permanent
Endowment Fund shall be expended for any purpos e and income
fr0tn the principal shall be used only for the maintenance
and general operation of Masonic Homes.

NOTE 2 • PRlOR PERIOD ADJUSTMENTS:

'Ihe ba lance sheet, statement of support, revenue and expenses and
changes in fund balances have been restated as of June 30, 1979, June JO,
1980 and.years then ended . 'Ihe restatement was necessary to give effect to
changes in accounting methods which r ecogni~e depreciation and employee
vacation compensation earned but unpaid. In addition, t he cost of buildings
and equipment at June 30, 1980 and June 30, 1981 have been r es tate d to give
effect to depreciated re placemen t c osts as detennined by independent appraisor s.

Res tricted Trust Fund - Details co this Trust fund are
contained in Note 7 to the financia l statement s.
Land, Buildings and Equipment:
Land is reported at cost. Buildings and equipment existing at
June 30, 1980 and June 30, 1981 are reported at depreciated replacement cost as determined by independent appraisors (9ee Note 2).
Depreciation is recorded by the straight-line method over t he
following estimated lives:

and equipment are capitalized. On sale or retirement, the cost and accu:;lated depreciation applicable thereto a re eliminated from the ac counts a

The Roy G. Jones Trust Fund:
All income from this trust is to be paid to a beneficiary for the
duration of her life. Masonic Homes of California holds a 50% remainder
interest in the assets.
Santa Fe Masonic Club Fund:
Ninety percent of the income from this trust is to be distributed
to Covina Children as cash gifts during the annual Christmae Party. The
remaining income is to be retained for fund growth.

NOTE S - PENS 10N PU.N:
The Masonic Homes of California contributes to the California HalOQl
Retirement Plan for the benefit of all eligible employees. The total peflllClllc
expense for the years ended June 30, 1981 and 1980 was $99,134 and $76,750
respectively. The Plan is fully funded.
NOTE 6 - LIFE ANNUITY AGREEMENT:
On November 27, 1974, Masonic Homes of California, in exchange fot
conveyance of real property, entered into an agreement to pay the conveyota
during their lifetime $1,250 per month. The recipients are presently 81 alld
85 years old and the liability at June 30, 1981 equals the present value of
future estimated payments, based upon life expectancies.

Details to each Trust Fund, foll""':

The principal and income of this fund is to be used for the benefit

Hildred R. Brown and Leroy C. Brown Memorial Fund:
Principal and income from this fund are to be used fo r making
loans for educational purposes to any children that the Board of Trustee s

George F. and Laura E. Brigham Scholarship Fund:
The principal of this fund is held as a scholarship fund for the
benefit of the Covina Home residents, of which $25,000 may be loaned for thl•
purpose. Income of this fund is restricted and may be used only for providing scholarships.
The F.

o. Hardy MelDOrial for Higher Practical Education:

Tile assets, liabilities and fund balances of the Temple are reported
in two self-balancing funds, as follows:

general operations of the Temple.
Learning Center and Temple Expansion Fund Resources are restricted for the creation of a
learning center and the expansion of the existing
Masonic Memorial Temple.

Land, buildings and equipment are carried at cost and , except for
land, are depreciated on the straight-line method over estimated useful
lives of 50 years for Temple buildings and equipment, 20 years for furnishings and 10 years for sound and lighting equipment. Maintenance and
repairs are charged to expense when incurred. Bettennents of a major
nature, which extend the useful lives of buildings and equipment, are
capitali%ed. On sale or retirement, the cost and acculll.llated depreciation
applicable thereto are eliminated from the accounts and the difference
between net b ook value and the proceeds from sale or retirement are
included in income.

NOTE l - ORGANIZATION:
The Masonic Homes Pooled Income FUnd was organized on
October 15, 1974 and is a charitable remainder trus t to which donors
contribute irrevocable remainder intere sts in property while retaining
an income interest for life for one or mo r e beneficiaries. The donors
are entitled t o a tax deduction equ ivalent t o the present value of the
re11111 inder inte r est in the property contributed.
The property transferred by such donor is held in trust by the
Board of Tru stees of the Masonic Homes Pooled Income FUnd and is comingled wit h and invested and reinvested with o ther properties transf er red t o the Fund. All income of the FUnd is distributed quarterly
t o the bene fici a ries , based on their proportionate share of the Pool.
Upon the death of each donor's last income beneficiary, t he remainder
interest i s di s tributed to Masonic Home s of California, a charitable
c orpor at ion .
